sections.title: Foreword
sections.text: forewordtime alters all. it permeates through everything without reverence, ultimately destroying even the most fundamental bindings created by fate and destiny itself. the logical becomes irrational, the familiar uncanny, the matter-of-fact, wrong.you may have felt this, as you grew to know your parents as flawed men, as you watched them slowly decay and die; as your birthplace was changed- ravaged by war or the stupidity of its residents.you may have even seen it as the world changed, time and time again; and yet eerily, remains the same. as if some unseen hand, desperately trying to gather all the infinitely miniscule specs of sand, to pour them back into a shattered hourglass.but even that is not enough. nothing is.time alters all- there is no end, only change. relentless, merciless change towards the unknown, the uncanny, the preposterous and the obscene.vie against it as you like, support it even, ye disillusioned fools. eventually you will see time for what it really is.immortality. a fate far worse than death.

sections.title: Character Creation at a Glance
sections.text:
character creation at a glancecreate a character in this order:generate three seven-result arrays and choose one complete array.
assign its results to the six ordinary attributes and luck. record a sanity score of 18 and current sanity 18.
choose a player race, apply its adjustments and maximums, and choose a prime attribute when the race grants one.decide where the character was raised.
choose one starting job at level 1 and apply its starting package and level-1 features.
record the resulting starting languages, then choose starting skills, any granted feat, and dm-approved possessions.
after worn armor and every other starting choice are known, record the character's final starting values and personal details.

sections.title: Attribute Scores and Modifiers
sections.text:
attribute scores and modifiers
a character has six ordinary attributes: strength, dexterity, constitution, intelligence, wisdom, and charisma. each has an attribute score and an ability modifier.
the full attribute score measures the character's raw capacity. when a rule calls for an attribute check, roll d20; a result equal to or lower than the score after bonuses and penalties succeeds. most other rules use the ability modifier shown in the table.

a score of 25 receives the modifier that 26 would ordinarily provide. scores above 25 return to the normal progression: 26-27 is +8, 28-29 is +9, and 30-31 is +10. such values require an explicit extraordinary source and are not part of ordinary character generation.
every final ordinary player attribute must be at least 5. luck follows its separate generation rule and may receive a lower result. racial maximum, including any prime-attribute increase, limits normal permanent advancement. a specific magical or extraordinary effect may explicitly allow you to exceed it.

sections.title: What the Attributes Represent
sections.text:
what the attributes represent



attribute
meaning and principal uses



strength (str)
physical power and leverage. it governs ordinary melee attacks and damage, block, carrying capacity, and many physical maneuvers.


dexterity (dex)
agility, coordination, reaction speed, and physical precision. it governs initiative, ordinary ranged attacks, dodge, reflex saves, ride, and readily accessible equipment.


constitution (con)
health, endurance, recovery, and resistance to bodily harm. it determines base life points and contributes to physical energy, fortitude, running endurance, wound survival, and recovery.


intelligence (int)
learning, reasoning, disciplined concentration, and aptitude for acquiring skills. it governs spell concentration capacity and defensive casting and helps determine additional starting skill choices.


wisdom (wis)
judgment, awareness, magical reserve, and force of will. it governs will saves, the amount of magical energy granted by wisdom, magical energy recovery, and certain spell-preservation checks.


charisma (cha)
presence, expression, and force of personality. it governs social skills and the default difficulty classes of spells and abilities.


these are the attributes' principal uses. a skill, class, spell, talent, or other specific rule may use an attribute in another appropriate way.

sections.title: Luck and Sanity
sections.text:
luck and sanityluck. luck is generated alongside the six ordinary attributes. assign one of the character's seven generated results to luck. luck has no racial modifier, cannot be a prime attribute, and produces no ability modifier. its maximum is 18, or 19 when its generation roll showed four 6s.
luck measures favorable or unfavorable uncertainty. when the dm calls for a luck check, roll d20 equal to or below the adjusted luck score. bonuses raise the effective threshold and penalties lower it. luck may determine whether a misplaced item is found, whether a plausible improvised tool is nearby, whether an appropriately trained character can locate a possible environmental resource, or which of several reasonable encounter circumstances occurs. it cannot create something impossible or replace relevant knowledge and training. failure may establish an unfavorable circumstance.
luck also provides a small reserve of character-saving rerolls:



luck score
luck rerolls per story arc

16-17

the dm decides when a new story arc begins and these uses refresh. a story arc may span a substantial period of play; luck does not refresh each session, day, or encounter.
after seeing the result of one of your own d20 rolls, spend one luck reroll to roll it again and keep whichever result is more favorable. if advantage or disadvantage applied, reroll one chosen die, resolve the revised roll, and keep the more favorable complete result. before making a disadvantaged roll, you may instead spend one use to cancel the remaining disadvantage and roll one ordinary d20. damage dice and other non-d20 rolls are not normally eligible, but the dm may permit an exception when the requested intervention is genuinely a matter of luck. luck has no other universal benefit.sanity score and current sanity. sanity is not generated or assigned and produces no ability modifier. every new character begins with a sanity score of 18 and current sanity 18.
sanity score is the permanent measure of the character's connection to ordinary reality, what they regard as normal, and how much horror or hardship they have absorbed. it sets maximum current sanity. current sanity is a separate hp-like pool that receives sanity damage. ordinary sanity damage reduces current sanity without reducing the permanent score.
severe experiences can permanently lower sanity score, representing both lasting damage and hardening. when this happens, maximum current sanity falls with it. if current sanity exceeds the new maximum, reduce it to that maximum; otherwise leave it unchanged. a character whose sanity score falls from 18 to 14 while at current sanity 12 remains at 12. one who was at current sanity 16 falls to 14.
lower sanity can make a character less vulnerable to familiar bloodshed, death, filth, and hardship, while making them increasingly alienated from ordinary society. high sanity is therefore not simply better than low sanity.
18: the ordinary starting point: a broadly normal upbringing without close participation in killing, murder, disease, or extreme conditions.
17-16: meaningful hardship without losing ordinary social function. violent bereavement or living through a damaged city may fall here.
15-14: substantial direct exposure to war, killing, blood, filth, lost comrades, or repulsive acts committed to survive.
around 12: hardening is visible in habits and outlook. self-care or possessions may be neglected, tics may emerge, and the character has reconciled themselves to conclusions that more sheltered people would reject.
10 or lower: the character is becoming genuinely dysfunctional in ordinary society, and other people can readily perceive that something is deeply wrong.
8-7: the character normally approaches or crosses the boundary of playability because severe trauma-driven or socially incompatible behavior prevents ordinary social function.
these values are interpretive anchors, not mandatory biographies or automatic behavior packages.

sections.title: Sanity checks and damage
sections.text:
sanity checks and damage. the dm may call for a sanity check when an event meaningfully defies the character's understanding of reality or exceeds what their history has normalized. the dm gives the event an implicit qualitative sanity threshold. if the character's sanity score is equal to or below that threshold, the character is sufficiently hardened and makes no check. a lower threshold represents a more extreme event because it can affect more heavily hardened characters.
if a check is required, roll d20. the character must roll higher than their sanity score to remain unaffected. failure inflicts sanity damage and reduces current sanity. this unusual roll deliberately makes high-sanity characters more sensitive once an event qualifies, while hardened characters are less likely to react to familiar mundane horror.
sanity damage has no fixed severity table. the dm considers the event, its implicit threshold, the character's sanity score and history, the distance between that score and the threshold, and the surrounding circumstances. mild shock commonly inflicts 1d6 sanity damage, moderate shock commonly inflicts 1d10, and severe or overwhelming shock may inflict several dice or another appropriate amount.recovery. current sanity recovers through genuinely calming, grounding, reassuring, or pleasurable experiences appropriate to the character. gambling, visiting a brothel, resting beside a river, wandering open plains, or watching the sun rise after a horrific night may all help, usually restoring 1d6 sanity. one ordinary night's rest does not automatically refill current sanity. long periods of safe downtime generally restore it fully, while a dungeon expedition, military campaign, or other sustained crisis does not. abilities and divine effects may also restore current sanity, especially when they remove or reframe the cause of the horror. exact recovery remains contextual and dm-adjudicated. as an example, the dm may assign xd6 sanity 'healing' when a character has had a good chance to recover, or full when they've had a good, long break from stressful circumstances/adventuring. sanity shocked. when current sanity reaches 0, the character becomes sanity shocked and rolls d20 equal to or below half their sanity score.on success, the character becomes resolute for the remainder of the encounter or approximately one hour, whichever better fits the situation. resolute fully restores current sanity, grants +4 to appropriate

sections.title: Generate Three Arrays
sections.text:
generate three arrays
generate three complete arrays, each containing seven results. generate every result as follows:
roll 4d6.
if one or more dice show 1, choose one of those dice and reroll it once. keep the new result even if it is another 1. do not reroll any other dice showing 1.
drop the lowest die and total the other three.
if all four dice show 6, the result is 19 rather than 18.
repeat this procedure until the array contains seven results, then generate two more complete arrays in the same way.

sections.title: Choose and Assign One Array
sections.text:
choose and assign one array
choose one of the three complete arrays and discard the other two. results cannot be exchanged or combined between arrays.
assign the chosen array's seven results freely among strength, dexterity, constitution, intelligence, wisdom, charisma, and luck. sanity is not assigned; it begins at 18.

sections.title: Racial Modifiers and Maximums
sections.text:
apply racial modifiers and maximums
after assigning the array, choose a race from the next section and apply its adjustments. each racial profile lists the maximum a member of that race can normally reach in each attribute. the same number determines the character's starting adjustment: subtract 20 from the listed maximum.
a listed maximum of 22 adds +2 to the assigned result.
a listed maximum of 19 applies -1 to the assigned result.
a listed maximum of 20 makes no change.
a human also chooses one prime attribute from strength, dexterity, constitution, intelligence, wisdom, or charisma. add +3 to both its starting value and permanent maximum. a half-elf chooses one prime attribute in the same way and adds +1 instead. luck and sanity cannot be prime attributes.
apply adjustments in this order: assign the generated result, apply the racial adjustment, then apply any prime-attribute increase. every resulting attribute must be at least 5. try another assignment or another generated array if one falls below 5. if none of the three arrays can keep every attribute at 5 or higher, generate three new arrays.
the racial maximum prevents ordinary permanent advancement beyond it. a miracle, wish, or similarly extraordinary effect may explicitly exceed that maximum.

sections.title: Reading a Racial Profile
sections.text:
reading a racial profilethe six attribute values in a racial profile show the race's ordinary permanent maximums. they also determine its starting adjustments, as explained in apply racial modifiers and maximums above.
size determines which size rules apply. speed is the distance the character can cover with ordinary movement. the me multiplier determines how much maximum magical energy the character gains from wisdom. multiply permanent wisdom by this number and round down. if permanent wisdom changes, calculate this amount again, then add any fixed me bonuses.
magic protection (mp) is passive protection that reduces spell damage by its listed amount. it is not magical energy and cannot be spent.

sections.title: Human
sections.text:
human
humans are vanaheim's most adaptable people. their nations and traditions differ enormously, and humans can master almost any calling. their defining strength is the speed with which they learn, specialize, and advance.
choose one prime attribute from str, dex, con, int, wis, or cha. add +3 to both its starting value and permanent maximum.
begin with one ordinary feat for which the character qualifies and one additional starting skill selection.
gain +1 xp after every session that awards xp.
a human who begins play as a mage gains +5 me. beginning as an acolyte does not grant this bonus, and choosing a mage job later does not grant it.

sections.title: Half-Elf
sections.text:
half-elf
half-elves combine human adaptability with elven longevity. they ordinarily mature near a human pace until roughly age 35 to 40, after which aging slows dramatically. no one can reliably predict a half-elf's lifespan: some live for centuries, some for far longer, and some may be immortal. near the final portion of life, the skin begins to harden and crack like bark and the hair loses color, though the half-elf rarely develops the frail appearance of a very old human.
choose one prime attribute from str, dex, con, int, wis, or cha. add +1 to both its starting value and permanent maximum.
gain low-light vision.
low-light vision: in dim light, double the distance at which the half-elf can see, to a maximum of 200 feet and never farther than the same scene could be seen in daylight. low-light vision provides no sight in total darkness.

sections.title: Elf
sections.text:
elf
the shared elf profile covers sylvar, pyran, and common elves. sylvar are the oldest and most otherworldly elven people; pyran are protective forest-dwellers shaped by long contact with humanity; common elves descend from pyran communities that lived among humans for generations. elves are immortal in lifespan but can be killed. they retain a young-adult appearance rather than becoming visibly elderly, and chronological age need not match apparent age.
an elf player character must have a good alignment.
gain sneak, low-light vision, racial detect magic, elven reverie and sleep immunity, mana well, and cold-iron weakness.
an ordinary elf has speed 30 feet. a pyran elf instead has speed 35 feet. unless another rule says otherwise, sylvar, pyran, and common elves share the same racial traits.
sneak (talent): an elf with sneak automatically succeeds on stealth checks against creatures that are not actively on guard, provided the elf remains outside their immediate line of sight. if the elf also possesses the hide talent, hide grants +10 on stealth while perfectly still in a place where hiding is physically possible; sneak allows the elf to move while retaining that bonus so long as concealment still permits stealth. detect invisibility reveals an elf using hide.
low-light vision: in dim light, double the distance at which the elf can see, to a maximum of 200 feet and never farther than the same scene could be seen in daylight. low-light vision provides no sight in total darkness.
racial detect magic: the elf can invoke the detect magic spell by concentrating. invoking it costs the same me and uses the same spell speed, concentration rules, and effect as the spell, but requires no verbal, somatic, or material components.
elven reverie and sleep immunity: elves are immune to mundane and magical sleep. instead of sleeping, an elf spends four hours in quiet elven reverie, recalling memories without dreaming. reverie satisfies the need for sleep and refreshes mana well; it does not prevent fatigue, exhaustion, or unconsciousness from another cause. recovering me, hp, pe, and physical fatigue still requires the full rest period specified by those rules; the four hours of reverie may occur within it.

sections.title: Dwarf
sections.text:
dwarf
dwarves are broad-built, long-lived people renowned for metalwork, stonecraft, and engineering. wars with the dark elves shattered most of their ancient underground realms, leaving relatively few free communities on the surface or beneath it; vaelrain remains one of the surviving free underground settlements. dwarves commonly live for approximately 300 to 400 years.
a dwarf is medium and has speed 30 feet.
gain infravision.
infravision: the dwarf perceives heat patterns within 60 feet, including in darkness. infravision does not reveal cold detail that produces no meaningful temperature contrast.

sections.title: Dark Elf
sections.text:
dark elf
dark elves are the evil-aligned inversion of the surface elven peoples, born from an ancient elven betrayal and now found primarily beneath the surface. a dark elf npc may possess additional traits listed in its creature profile.
sneak (talent): a dark elf with sneak automatically succeeds on stealth checks against creatures that are not actively on guard, provided the dark elf remains outside their immediate line of sight. if the dark elf also possesses the hide talent, hide grants +10 on stealth while perfectly still in a place where hiding is physically possible; sneak allows the dark elf to move while retaining that bonus so long as concealment still permits stealth. detect invisibility reveals a dark elf using hide.
infravision: the dark elf perceives heat patterns within 60 feet, including in darkness. infravision does not reveal cold detail that produces no meaningful temperature contrast.

sections.title: Gnome
sections.text:
gnome
gnomes use the statistics above. a gnome's creature profile supplies its speed and racial abilities. gnomes are exceptionally rare, so their details do not belong in this book.

sections.title: Sprite
sections.text:
sprite
sprites are ageless magical beings whose maximum me is also their life force. outside a place with sufficiently abundant ambient magic, each sprite people loses maximum me at the rate stated by its profile. a sprite dies if its maximum me reaches 0; its animating being and soul are gone rather than merely resting or unconscious.
low-light vision: in dim light, double the distance at which the sprite can see, to a maximum of 200 feet and never farther than the same scene could be seen in daylight. low-light vision provides no sight in total darkness.
racial detect magic: the sprite can invoke the detect magic spell by concentrating. invoking it costs the same me and uses the same spell speed, concentration rules, and effect as the spell, but requires no verbal, somatic, or material components.
cold-iron weakness: sprites are vulnerable to cold iron. after applicable protection reduces a cold-iron attack's damage, add half the remaining damage, rounding down, before physical energy mitigation. if protection reduces the damage to 0, the weakness creates no damage.
sand runners: sand runners remain npc-only in the current core rules. they are medium, human-sized sprites with subtly different eyes, slightly sharper teeth, and wings that fold beneath clothing. a sand runner outside sufficiently abundant magic loses 1 maximum me per month. returning to abundant magic allows that loss to recover, but the creature profile or dm determines the rate. use the sand runner's creature profile for its land speed, flying speed, and other abilities.

sections.title: Giant
sections.text:
giant
giants retain their large build and speed 30 feet. a giant's creature profile lists any exceptional abilities it possesses, such as bash, enhanced damage, or boulder.

sections.title: Choose One Starting Job
sections.text:
choose one starting job
choose one job from classes whose entry requirements the character satisfies. the character begins at job level 1 and overall level 1 with no unspent xp. restricted jobs require the permission stated in their profiles.
apply everything explicitly granted by the job's starting package and its other level-1 features. a rank or talent-access list shows what the character may learn or purchase. entries on that list are not gained automatically unless the job says otherwise.
if the starting job belongs to the acolyte family, choose its permanent hp, me, or balanced progression now. if a human's starting job belongs to the mage family, add the human's +5 me after applying the ordinary mage level-1 me gain.

sections.title: Starting Skills and Languages
sections.text:
starting skills and languages
every character begins fluent in one regional language associated with where the character was raised. the regional languages used for character creation are ayamaoan, taslamaran, uxmaln, zhenshi, aghelian, and imperial. vanaheim has no universal common language.
an elf also begins fluent in sylvan.
a dwarf also begins fluent in deep tongue.
a sprite also begins fluent in sylvan, though sprites remain npc-only in the current core rules.
a character whose starting job belongs to the mage family also begins fluent in arcane.
these granted languages are trained knowledge (language: specific language) fields and use no starting skill choices. every additional language is learned as a separate knowledge (language: specific language) skill and uses one starting skill choice unless another rule grants it. learning a special language during creation requires dm permission and appropriate access.
after recording the granted languages, choose starting skills in this order:
choose three skills appropriate to the training of the starting job, subject to dm approval.
add unrestricted skill choices equal to the character's positive permanent intelligence modifier after racial and prime-attribute adjustments. a modifier of +0 or lower adds no choices and never removes any of the three job-based choices.
a human adds one further unrestricted skill choice.
skills cannot be purchased twice. every separately named craft, knowledge, performance, or profession field is a different skill. these choices grant trained skills, not skill masteries, and acquiring another job later does not re-grant them. a character may spend an eligible choice on an additional language as described above.

sections.title: Starting Talents and Equipment
sections.text:
starting talents and equipmentrecord every automatic racial and job feature. a human also chooses one ordinary feat for which the character qualifies. complete feat and talent choices use talents and feats; access to a talent is permission to learn it, not an automatic grant.
the dm or the adventure supplies or approves starting possessions. equipment training permits the character to use the named equipment. character creation supplies no universal starting wealth or item package.
choose worn armor before calculating final maximum hp because armor hp increases the wearer's one hp pool while the armor is worn.

sections.title: Record Starting Values
sections.text:
record starting values
after the character's race, starting job, skills, languages, feat, talents, and possessions are known, record the following maximums and starting statistics:



value
starting calculation



attributes
record each final score and its ability modifier. also record luck, a sanity score of 18, and current sanity 18.


size and speed
use the racial profile.


lp
maximum lp equals permanent constitution unless an explicit effect changes it.


hp
begin with 1 hp for a warrior or for an acolyte who chose the hp path. adventurers, mages, and acolytes on the me or balanced path begin with 0 hp. add worn armor's armor hp and any other stated increase.


pe
maximum pe begins at 4 plus constitution modifier, followed by any stated bonus. maximum pe cannot be lower than 0.


me
multiply permanent wisdom by the race's me multiplier and round down. add 1 me for a mage or for an acolyte who chose the me path. warrior, adventurer, and the acolyte hp and balanced paths add 0 me at level 1. then add every other stated increase.


magic protection
record the racial value and any explicit additional protection.


bab and saves
bab and the three base saves begin at 0. add constitution modifier to fortitude, dexterity modifier to reflex, and wisdom modifier to will, followed by explicit starting-package bonuses.


features and possessions
record racial traits, job features, trained skills, languages, the human feat when applicable, equipment permissions, and every carried or worn item.


a human starting mage adds 6 me to the wisdom-derived amount: 1 from mage progression and 5 from the human starting-mage benefit. a starting acolyte's permanent progression choice determines whether level 1 contributes hp, me, or neither on the balanced path.

sections.title: Character Details
sections.text:
character details
record the character's name, appearance, home region, alignment, faith or patron when relevant, and any other brief personal details desired for play.

sections.title: Classes & Jobs
sections.text: classesclasses and jobs14classes · classes and jobsclassesunderstanding classes and jobsclass familiesthe four ordinary class families are warrior, adventurer, acolyte, and mage. a family groups jobs that share a broad advancement chassis and occupies one of the four ordinary family positions available to a character.jobsa job is a level-bearing class within one class family. each job has its own level, unlock track, job features, talent access, and any spell access printed in its profile.the current core jobs are:class familycurrent jobswarriormercenary, swashbuckler, barbarianadventurerscout, rogue, bardacolytepriest, shaman, paladin, hellionmagesorcerer, warlock, necromancer (restricted; dm permission)this is the current core-book roster. necromancer is included so readers can understand the path, but it is not an ordinary starting choice. the roster does not claim that no other training exists in the setting.training beyond the core jobssome organizations and traditions teach level-bearing paths beyond the thirteen core jobs. those paths belong to the separate gm and beyond expansion; their individual requirements, progression, and interactions remain outside this core chapter.talent access and exclusive talentsevery named entry in a job's rank table is a talent, even when its name resembles an ordinary competency. a talent may call for, modify, replace, or automatically resolve a skill check, but that interaction does not turn the talent  into an ordinary skill. skills are governed separately by the skills rules.a character may learn a class talent only when one of their jobs lists that talent, the talent explicitly lists their job or class family as eligible, or another explicit rule grants access. training supplies the method of learning an eligible talent; it does not grant access by itself.an exclusive talent may be learned only through its named job unless an explicit rule says otherwise. exclusive controls who may learn a talent. it is separate from class mastery, which controls whether a signature combat engine can operate alongside one learned from another job.class masteriesa class mastery is a job's signature combat engine. a character can know class masteries from several jobs but may use only one during a round.

sections.title: Mercenary
sections.text: classesmercenary24classes · mercenarymercenaryidentity and role. mercenaries are vanaheim's professional soldiers: campaign veterans, household retainers, caravan guards, town watchmen, and sellswords whose loyalties differ but whose trade is trained combat. the name describes a broad military profession, not one company or allegiance. mercenaries rely on extensive equipment training, dependable battlefield discipline, and practiced mastery of chosen weapons.progression. mercenaries use shared advancement and the warrior chassis above. a mercenary's ordinary attack speed is 1 for both armed and unarmed combat unless an explicit talent or other rule increases it.starting packageequipment training. acquiring mercenary job level 1 grants training with axe, bow, crossbow, dagger, flail, mace, polearm, sling, spear, staff, sword, whip, and unarmed combat. it also grants training with all ordinary shields and light, medium, and heavy armor. this does not supply culturally restricted, specialist, item-specific, firearm, rifle, pistol, siege-weapon, or other explicitly exceptional training.war etiquette. the mercenary gains +4 on charisma-based social checks involving soldiers, guards, commanders, and other military-trained personnel.apprentice talent access. bash and enhanced damage become available for purchase. neither talent is learned automatically.class talentsthe rank table below lists every talent available through the mercenary job. only the talents most important to understanding how the job fights are explained here. complete descriptions and xp costs for the remaining talents appear in talents and feats.mercenary ranktalent accessapprenticebash; enhanced damagejourneymandirt kick; hard trip; self defense; fast healing; endurance; rescueveteransecond attack; disarm; kick; brawling; retreatexpertrallying cry; haggle; skirmish; weapon mastery imentorweapon mastery ii; third attackmasterblitzkrieg; weapon mastery iiiretreat. retreat is a purchased veteran talent that allows a mercenary to organize willing allies into a coordinated withdrawal. the participants commit their turns to the maneuver; on success, the formation moves up to 100 feet without provoking attacks of opportunity. the complete formation requirements, knowledge (tactics) procedure, level bonus, opposing-commander interaction, failure result, and xp cost appear under retreat in talents and feats.rallying cry. rallying cry is an exclusive expert talent. the mercenary uses it as a free action, spends 2 pe, and must be participating in group combat or immediately preparing the group for battle. the mercenary and allies who can hear and understand the cry gain a morale bonus equal to the mercenary's charisma modifier on attack and active defense rolls for 1 minute. at master rank, the recipients also gain +0.5 attack speed beginning at the start of the next round.multiple rallying cries do not stack; use the greatest applicable bonus. rallying cry's temporary attack-speed increase does not stack with another temporary effect-based attack-speed increase such as haste or bard song; use the greatest applicable increase. rallying cry remains available when another class mastery is selected.

sections.title: Swashbuckler
sections.text: classesswashbuckler26classes · swashbucklerswashbuckleridentity and role. swashbucklers are duelists and mobile skirmishers who value speed, nerve, and individual technique over formation fighting. they use paired weapons, rapid footwork, and an opponent's failed attack to seize momentum, making them especially dangerous when they have room to move. across vanaheim, the title covers several traditions of individual swordsmanship rather than one uniform school. swashbucklers appear among household champions, irregular companies, mobile officers, and professional duelists, where timing, footwork, nerve, and individual initiative matter more than formation discipline.progression. swashbucklers use shared advancement and the warrior chassis above. a swashbuckler's ordinary armed attack speed is 1 unless an explicit talent or other rule increases it.starting packageequipment training. acquiring swashbuckler job level 1 grants training with dagger, one-handed axe, sword, whip, sling, bow, crossbow, and unarmed combat. it also grants training with light armor and the buckler. specialist, culturally restricted, and item-specific equipment still requires its own training.sword supremacy. while wielding two sword-group weapons, the swashbuckler gains +2 to initiative and improves the critical-threat range of those swords by 1. when a large or smaller opponent connects with a melee attack against the swashbuckler, reduce its positive attack margin by 2, to a minimum of 0. this happens after the hit is established and cannot turn a hit into a miss. it reduces only the margin added to damage; it is not damage reduction.suave. the swashbuckler gains +4 on charisma-based checks made to blend into a loosely organized group. apply -4 instead when attempting to blend into a disciplined organization with an established order, such as an army or paladin order. this modifies the attempt to blend into the group, not every charisma check involving its members.quick draw. the swashbuckler may draw an accessible one-handed sword-group weapon without spending movement. this remains available when another class mastery is selected. it does not accelerate sheathing or retrieving a stored weapon.apprentice talent access. dirt kick, dual wield, heckle, self defense, and juggle become available for purchase. none are learned automatically.class talentsthe rank table below lists every talent available through the swashbuckler job. only the talents most important to understanding how the job fights are explained here. complete descriptions and xp costs for the remaining talents appear in talents and feats.swashbuckler ranktalent accessapprenticedirt kick; sections.title: Barbarian
sections.text: classesbarbarian · class talents30classes · barbarianbarbarianidentity and role. barbarian is a broad rules name for warriors shaped by frontier, clan, and spirit-venerating traditions beyond the formal schools of the great powers. it describes no single nation or people. their fighting style channels endurance and deliberate battle-fury, while their upbringing often preserves old folklore and courtesies toward the spirits that predate human religion.progression. barbarians use shared advancement and the warrior chassis above. a barbarian's ordinary attack speed is 1 for both armed and unarmed combat unless an explicit talent or other rule increases it.starting packageequipment training. acquiring barbarian job level 1 grants training with axe, bow, dagger, flail, mace, polearm, sling, spear, staff, sword, whip, and unarmed combat. it also grants light and medium armor training and training with the buckler, standard shield, and heavy shield. it does not grant crossbow, heavy armor, pavise, firearm, siege-weapon, culturally restricted, specialist, or item-specific training.berserk. the barbarian gains berserk at job level 1. its complete activation, duration, benefits, and ending procedure appears under class mastery: berserk and fury below.old courtesy. the pre-human spirits lost territory and influence as human gods and temples spread, leaving many skeptical of organized human worship without making them automatically hostile. the barbarian gains +4 on charisma-based social checks made directly with those spirits, shamans, and mortal communities that actively venerate them. this familiarity does not detect spirits, supply a language, compel assistance, improve a spirit's attitude automatically, provide safe passage, or grant a magical ability. it does not extend to gods, divine servants, undead, ancestors, or every supernatural creature called a spirit.hearth wisdom. the barbarian gains +2 on intelligence-based checks to recall folklore, old stories, local legends, traditional warnings, and remembered customs associated with a place or people. apply the intelligence modifier normally and then add this bonus. hearth sections.title: Adventurer Jobs
sections.text: classesadventurer jobs34classes · adventurer jobsadventurer jobsadventurer chassisthe adventurer family contains the scout, rogue, and bard jobs. all three use the universal base-save cap and adventurer save costs under shared advancement, together with the adventurer train caps. an adventurer gains 1 hp and 1 me at every two adventurer job levels.once per battle, when making one damage roll, an adventurer may add their adventurer job level to that roll. this is one fixed addition to one chosen damage roll. it is not added to every attack in a full attack, does not repeat across an area or ongoing effect, and is not itself a damage die multiplied by a critical hit or another dice multiplier. apply it as part of raw damage before damage reduction, pe mitigation, and hp or lp routing.this adventurer-chassis ability is unavailable during round 0 and becomes available when round 1 begins. it is not a class mastery and may work alongside a job's chosen mastery when both abilities are otherwise legal.the adventurer chassis grants no equipment training, wilderness feature, extra attack, attack speed increase, quick draw, class mastery, or specific talent access. those belong to the individual jobs and talents that grant them.

sections.title: Scout
sections.text: classesscout36classes · scoutscoutidentity and role. scouts are pathfinders, hunters, outriders, and reconnaissance specialists who operate ahead of armies and beyond settled roads. they read terrain, survive with little support, move among frontier communities, and try to decide an encounter with a concealed first shot before settling into disciplined ranged combat.progression. scouts use shared advancement and the adventurer chassis above. a scout's ordinary attack speed is 1 for both armed and unarmed combat unless an explicit talent or other rule increases it.starting packageequipment training. acquiring scout job level 1 grants training with spear, axe, dagger, bow, crossbow, staff, sword, whip, and unarmed combat. it also grants training with light armor and the buckler. it does not grant medium or heavy armor, larger shields, firearms, siege weapons, athani blackbows, gravity balls, culturally restricted equipment, or another specialist or item-specific training. an item that requires its own special training still requires that training.endurance. the scout gains endurance at job level 1 and uses its warrior-style pe schedule for qualifying scout levels unless pathfinding later replaces that rate with the scout-specific progression below.tracking. the scout gains tracking at job level 1. tracking uses its own procedure when circumstances require a check; possessing it does not turn every sign into an automatic success.trailcraft. when uncertainty requires a check, trailcraft uses survival. the scout gains +4 on survival checks to find food or water, choose safe shelter, predict ordinary weather, and recognize natural travel hazards. trailcraft does not find or follow another creature's trail, prevent the scout from becoming lost, or replace tracking or pathfinding.frontier manners. the scout gains +4 on charisma-based social checks involving hunters, trappers, wilderness guides, isolated settlements, and other people whose lives depend upon frontier or wilderness travel. this is not a general bonus with every rural person and does not guarantee hospitality, trust, supplies, or safe passage.scout camouflage. the scout gains scout camouflage at job level 1. its complete preparation and concealment procedure appears immediately below.apprentice talent access. butcher, sneak, tame, and fletch become available for purchase. none are learned automatically.scout camouflagethe scout may spend 10 minutes preparing camouflage from materials appropriate to the current terrain. while it remains matched to that terrain, the scout gains +20 on stealth checks to remain hidden. this bonus does not stack with hide's +10; use the greater applicable bonus.the scout may remain stationary normally. if the scout also possesses sneak, movement made while sneaking does not end the camouflage. otherwise movement ends it. attacking, casting a spell, taking another conspicuous action, or leaving the matching terrain ends the camouflage after the action resolves.scout camouflage is physical concealment rather than invisibility. detect invisibility does not reveal the scout, and ordinary scent-based detection cannot locate the scout through the camouflage alone. tremorsense and another sense that directly detects the scout's movement or physical contact with the ground still function normally. the +20 remains a stealth modifier rather than automatic success.class talentsthe rank table below lists every talent available through the scout job. only the selected talents and job-owned procedures most important to understanding how the scout operates are explained here. complete generic descriptions and xp costs for the remaining talents appear in talents and feats.

sections.title: Rogue
sections.text: classesrogue40classes · roguerogueidentity and role. rogues are infiltrators, thieves, assassins, fixers, and other specialists who win through preparation, misdirection, and control over when violence begins. they excel when an enemy is unaware, exposed, or occupied; a fair prolonged exchange gives up the advantages on which their training depends.progression. rogues use shared advancement and the adventurer chassis above. a rogue's ordinary armed and unarmed attack speed is 1 unless an explicit weapon configuration, talent, or other rule increases it.starting packageequipment training. acquiring rogue job level 1 grants training with dagger, mace, sword, whip, sling, bow, crossbow, and unarmed combat. it also grants training with light armor and the buckler. it does not grant medium or heavy armor, larger shields, culturally restricted equipment, or another specialist or item-specific training. an item that requires its own special training still requires that training.finesse. the rogue may use dexterity in place of strength for attack, weapon damage, and parry with a light or medium melee weapon. dexterity replaces strength in each applicable formula; the two modifiers are not added together. finesse remains available when another class mastery is selected.quick draw. the rogue may draw an accessible light or medium melee weapon eligible for finesse without spending movement. quick draw remains available when another class mastery is selected. it does not accelerate sheathing or retrieving a stored weapon.casing. the rogue gains +4 on checks involving entrances, exits, patrol routines, escape routes, and likely access points in a built environment. casing gathers or interprets information available from observation; it does not automatically reveal a concealed route or security measure.underworld courtesy. the rogue gains +4 on charisma-based social checks involving thieves, smugglers, fences, and similar criminal operators. this familiarity does not guarantee trust, cooperation, favorable prices, membership, or safe passage.apprentice talent access. backstab, hard trip, haggle, hide, peek, and self defense become available for purchase. none are learned automatically.class talentsthe rank table below lists every talent available through the rogue job. only the job-defining procedures needed to understand how the rogue creates and exploits an advantage are explained here. complete generic descriptions and xp costs for the remaining talents appear in talents and feats.rogue ranktalent accessapprenticebackstab; hard trip; haggle; hide; peek; self defensejourneymansneak; steal; disguise; sneak attackveteranplant; brawling; hamstring; climb; enduranceexpertenhanced damage; second attack; dual backstab; skirmishmentorenvenom; featherfoot; street network; scrolls; staves; wandsmasterultimate evasionclass mastery: roguesneak attack, backstab, hamstring, and dual backstab form one package. they may work together when their individual requirements are met. selecting another job's class mastery suppresses every rogue-mastery benefit for that round. finesse, quick draw, casing, underworld courtesy, skirmish, envenom, and other non-mastery features or talents remain available under their own rules.if sneak attack or backstab first becomes relevant through an opening attack, lock or choose rogue mastery immediately before that attack roll. rogue mastery may therefore be selected during round 0 when one of its abilities is otherwise legal.sneak attack and backstab each grant the same +1 pen increase. these increases do not stack: an attack qualifying for both gains +1 pen total, not +2.

sections.title: Attribute Checks and Skill Checks
sections.text: attribute checks and skill checksmost ordin­ary activ­ity needs no roll. make a check when the result is genu­inely uncer­tain and success or failure matters.an attrib­ute check resolves some­thing a plaus­ible char­ac­ter could attempt without a named body of train­ing. roll d20 equal to or below the rel­ev­ant raw attrib­ute score after apply­ing dif­fi­culty and other mod­i­fi­ers.a skill check resolves a task gov­erned by a named skill. a trained char­ac­ter begins with the full rel­ev­ant attrib­ute score. a char­ac­ter who lacks the skill follows its untrained rule; the same task does not become an attrib­ute check merely because the untrained threshold is less favor­able.a short, ordin­ary jump may call for a dex­ter­ity check. a dif­fi­cult leap that requires trained body control may call for acro­bat­ics instead.

sections.title: Choosing the Governing Attribute
sections.text: choosing the governing attributeeach skill lists its usual attrib­ute, which is the normal start­ing point for its checks. the dm may choose another attrib­ute when the char­ac­ter genu­inely uses a dif­fer­ent method.intim­id­a­tion ordin­ar­ily uses cha­risma when the char­ac­ter relies on pres­ence, threats, or force of per­son­al­ity. a display of phys­ical menace may use strength instead. the skill remains intim­id­a­tion; only the attrib­ute gov­ern­ing that attempt changes.

sections.title: Trained and Untrained Use
sections.text: trained and untrained usea trained skill check begins with the full gov­ern­ing attrib­ute. an untrained attempt that the skill permits begins with half the gov­ern­ing attrib­ute, rounded down. apply dif­fi­culty and other mod­i­fi­ers after estab­lish­ing that start­ing threshold.the untrained line in each skill entry uses one of three labels:untrained meaning yes ordinary uses may be attempted untrained. limited basic or obvious uses may be attempted untrained. technical, professional, or hazardous uses require training. trained only the named skill use requires training. an ordinary nontechnical action may still be an attribute check when it does not require that body of knowledge. for example, a char­ac­ter with dex­ter­ity 15 begins a trained acro­bat­ics check at 15. if the attemp­ted use permits an untrained check, the char­ac­ter instead begins at 7 after round­ing down. normal dif­fi­culty lowers that untrained threshold to 5.

sections.title: Difficulty
sections.text: difficultyafter estab­lish­ing the check's start­ing threshold, apply the task's dif­fi­culty:difficulty easy normal hard very hard extreme modifier — -2 -4 -6 -8 easy rep­res­ents a mean­ing­ful check under favor­able or ordin­ary cir­cum­stances. normal intro­duces some risk or com­plic­a­tion. hard, very hard, and extreme rep­res­ent increas­ingly demand­ing cir­cum­stances, with extreme forming the prac­tical end of the ordin­ary ladder. a spe­cific skill, talent, spell, or other rule may state another mod­i­fier when its own pro­ced­ure requires one.bonuses raise the threshold; pen­al­ties and dif­fi­culty lower it. roll d20. a result equal to or below the final threshold suc­ceeds. natural 1 and natural 20 have no sep­ar­ate auto­matic effect on a roll-under check; compare the result with the threshold nor­mally. an unmod­i­fied threshold of 20 cannot fail an ordin­ary d20 check.

sections.title: Opposed Checks and Check Margin
sections.text: opposed checks and check marginwhen two char­ac­ters dir­ectly oppose one another, both make the required check. for each par­ti­cipant, sub­tract the d20 result from the adjus­ted threshold. the result is the char­ac­ter's check margin.the higher check margin wins, even when both margins are neg­at­ive. a tie favors the defender. check margin is sep­ar­ate from an attack's margin of success.when a rule says that an opposed check suc­ceeds by 8 or more, the winning check margin must exceed the losing margin by at least 8. in an unop­posed check, failure by 8 or more means a check margin of -8 or lower.example: opposed check marginsone par­ti­cipant has an adjus­ted threshold of 20 and rolls 23, pro­du­cing a check margin of -3. the other has a threshold of 18 and rolls 20, pro­du­cing a check margin of -2. both rolled above their thresholds, but -2 is the higher margin, so the second par­ti­cipant wins. if both margins were equal, the defender would win.

sections.title: Time, Attempts, and Repeated Effort
sections.text: time, attempts, and repeated efforta check takes however long the attemp­ted task nat­ur­ally requires. a spe­cific skill use, talent, combat option, or other rule states an exact action or dur­a­tion when timing matters.one roll ordin­ar­ily rep­res­ents the com­plete attempt. failure does not grant unlim­ited con­sequence-free rerolls through the same method. another attempt becomes pos­sible when the task nat­ur­ally permits repeated effort, but each attempt con­sumes its normal time and carries the cir­cum­stances and con­sequences of con­tinu­ing.a char­ac­ter may keep trying to force a door, for example, while every attempt takes time and makes noise. research­ing the same exhausted source again does not produce another answer unless the char­ac­ter brings new inform­a­tion, gains access to dif­fer­ent mater­ial, or changes the method.

sections.title: Skills and Talents
sections.text: skills and talentsskills describe learned, repeat­able com­pet­en­cies. talents grant excep­tional train­ing or abil­it­ies that may use, improve, replace, or auto­mat­ic­ally resolve a skill check.stealth remains the ordin­ary skill behind con­ceal­ment and quiet move­ment; hide and sneak provide their own excep­tional bene­fits. sur­vival sup­ports delib­er­ate exam­in­a­tion of tracks; the track­ing talent permits much faster recog­ni­tion and pursuit of usable signs. medi­cine covers dia­gnosis and con­tinu­ing care; field medic provides urgent treat­ment under field pres­sure.when a talent changes a skill, use the talent's com­plete rule. learn­ing the skill alone does not grant the talent, and learn­ing the talent does not trans­form it into a second skill.

sections.title: Starting Skills
sections.text: starting skillsa new char­ac­ter receives start­ing skills in three parts:choose three skills appro­pri­ate to the train­ing of the char­ac­ter's start­ing job. choose from the full skill cata­logue, subject to dm approval.add unres­tric­ted skill choices equal to the char­ac­ter's pos­it­ive per­man­ent intel­li­gence mod­i­fier after racial and prime-attrib­ute adjust­ments. a mod­i­fier of +0 or lower adds no choices and never removes any of the three job-based choices.a human adds one further unres­tric­ted skill choice.a repeated choice must be replaced rather than learned twice. each sep­ar­ately named craft, know­ledge, per­form­ance, or pro­fes­sion field is a sep­ar­ate skill. know­ledge (history) and know­ledge (lan­guage: ayamaoan), for example, are two dif­fer­ent choices.lan­guages granted by region, race, or a start­ing mage job cost no start­ing skill choices; char­ac­ter cre­ation lists those grants. every addi­tional lan­guage is its own know­ledge (lan­guage: spe­cific lan­guage) skill and uses one start­ing skill choice unless another rule grants it. learn­ing a special lan­guage during cre­ation requires dm per­mis­sion and appro­pri­ate access.start­ing skill choices grant trained skills, not skill mas­ter­ies. intel­li­gence determ­ines how many skill mas­ter­ies the char­ac­ter may even­tu­ally know; it does not grant those mas­ter­ies auto­mat­ic­ally. acquir­ing another job later does not repeat these cre­ation-only choices.

sections.title: Learning a New Skill
sections.text: learning a new skilllearn­ing a new skill after char­ac­ter cre­ation nor­mally costs 10 xp. the dm may raise the cost as high as 30 xp accord­ing to how dif­fi­cult or unfa­mil­iar that train­ing is for the char­ac­ter and the cir­cum­stances in which it is being learned.the char­ac­ter's exist­ing jobs, back­ground, exper­i­ence, access to inform­a­tion, and oppor­tun­ity to prac­tice all matter. a sor­cerer accus­tomed to lib­rar­ies and magical study may find sur­vival unusu­ally dif­fi­cult, while a career warrior may have the same dif­fi­culty learn­ing know­ledge (magic). this is a judg­ment made for the char­ac­ter and situ­ation, not a fixed com­pat­ib­il­ity table.a suit­able instructor may halve the final xp cost, to a minimum of 5 xp.

sections.title: Skill Mastery
sections.text: skill masterya skill mastery unlocks the advanced uses described in that skill's mastery inset. it grants no uni­ver­sal numer­ical bonus and never guar­an­tees success. when the outcome remains uncer­tain, roll the under­ly­ing skill nor­mally.a char­ac­ter must know a skill before learn­ing its mastery, and the mastery must be learned or pur­chased; it is never gained auto­mat­ic­ally. each skill's mastery can be learned only once and never stacks with itself.the number of skill mas­ter­ies a char­ac­ter may know cannot exceed the char­ac­ter's per­man­ent intel­li­gence mod­i­fier, with a minimum capa­city of one. tem­por­ary effects and equip­ment do not create addi­tional capa­city.learn­ing a skill mastery takes at least six months and ordin­ar­ily takes about one year. it requires proper tutel­age: a qual­i­fied teacher, a uni­ver­sity or com­par­able insti­tu­tion, or another source capable of provid­ing sus­tained advanced train­ing.a skill mastery costs between 10 and 30 xp, as determ­ined by the dm accord­ing to the field, the avail­able tutel­age, and the cir­cum­stances of the train­ing.

sections.title: Reading a Skill Entry
sections.text: reading a skill entryeach entry begins with the skill's usual attrib­ute and its untrained label. the usual attrib­ute governs most attempts, although a genu­inely dif­fer­ent method may call for another attrib­ute. the untrained label states whether a char­ac­ter without the skill may attempt all ordin­ary uses, only basic uses, or none of the named skill uses.the descrip­tion iden­ti­fies the tasks the skill com­monly governs. a related talent line appears when a con­firmed talent builds on that skill and helps the reader find the excep­tional pro­ced­ure. a skill mastery section appears only when that skill has a com­plete advanced-use rule.

sections.title: Acrobatics
sections.text: acrobaticsusual attribute: dexterity untrained: yesacro­bat­ics covers demand­ing move­ment that depends on balance, coordin­a­tion, and precise control. a char­ac­ter might use it to cross a narrow beam or rain-slick roof, keep footing on a swaying bridge, nego­ti­ate loose rubble, land under control after a dif­fi­cult drop, or place the body pre­cisely during a dif­fi­cult leap.use ath­let­ics when height, dis­tance, force, or sus­tained exer­tion is the central chal­lenge. acro­bat­ics applies when balance, place­ment, or a con­trolled landing matters most.related talent: tum­bling. tum­bling builds on acro­bat­ics for excep­tional move­ment.

sections.title: Animal Handling
sections.text: animal handlingusual attribute: wisdom untrained: yesanimal hand­ling governs imme­di­ate inter­ac­tion with an animal and the ability to read its present beha­vior. it may help a char­ac­ter approach a nervous horse, settle a pack animal frightened by noise or blood, lead live­stock through a crowded place, restrain an agit­ated dog, or recog­nize signs of fear, pain, aggres­sion, or exhaus­tion.the animal's tem­pera­ment, famili­ar­ity with the char­ac­ter, treat­ment, sur­round­ings, and current dis­tress shape the attempt. teach­ing lasting com­mands and prac­ticed beha­vior uses animal train­ing. when someone is already in the saddle, ride governs the rider's control while animal hand­ling remains rel­ev­ant when the animal's dis­pos­i­tion is the real dif­fi­culty.

sections.title: Animal Training
sections.text: animal trainingusual attribute: wisdom untrained: limitedanimal train­ing teaches lasting com­mands, estab­lishes routines, and accus­toms an animal to unfa­mil­iar demands. it can teach an animal to halt, return, carry a rider or load, accept harness, remain man­age­able around crowds or loud activ­ity, and perform work appro­pri­ate to its nature and train­ing.train­ing takes the time appro­pri­ate to the animal and the beha­vior being taught. tem­pera­ment, prior treat­ment, danger, and the com­plex­ity of the desired beha­vior shape the task.

sections.title: Appraisal
sections.text: appraisalusual attribute: intelligence untrained: limitedappraisal estim­ates an object's quality, con­di­tion, work­man­ship, authen­ti­city, and likely value. it can dis­tin­guish careful crafts­man­ship from dec­or­at­ive show, recog­nize repairs or sub­sti­tu­tions, compare two pieces of appar­ently similar quality, and judge whether an object matches its claimed mater­ial or origin.famil­iar goods and obvious defects may be judged untrained. train­ing becomes import­ant when value depends on rare mater­i­als, subtle work­man­ship, con­cealed repairs, spe­cial­ist con­struc­tion, or a con­vin­cing imit­a­tion.appraisal exam­ines the object itself. com­merce con­cerns the market, pro­spect­ive buyers, and terms of sale. a rel­ev­ant craft may reveal tech­nical flaws that a general appraisal cannot estab­lish.

sections.title: Athletics
sections.text: athleticsusual attribute: strength untrained: yesath­let­ics covers force­ful or sus­tained phys­ical move­ment. its ordin­ary uses include climb­ing a rough wall or rope, pulling oneself over a ledge, swim­ming through dif­fi­cult water, sprint­ing across demand­ing ground, clear­ing a ditch, or jumping high enough to seize a hand­hold.

sections.title: Bluff
sections.text: bluffusual attribute: charisma untrained: yesbluff lets a char­ac­ter present false­hood, mis­dir­ec­tion, or con­cealed intent as some­thing plaus­ible. it covers spoken lies, feigned con­fid­ence, mis­lead­ing beha­vior, inven­ted explan­a­tions, and dis­trac­tions created through words or conduct.a decep­tion becomes easier to believe when it fits what the listener already expects and agrees with the evid­ence at hand. firsthand know­ledge, obvious con­tra­dic­tions, close scru­tiny, or a story that demands too much faith make the attempt harder.at a city gate, a trav­eler might claim that a delayed wagon is expec­ted inside, answer ques­tions with rehearsed con­fid­ence, and keep the guard's atten­tion away from a com­pan­ion. pre­par­ing a false pass would call for forgery, while taking the guard's key would call for sleight of hand.

sections.title: Cartography
sections.text: cartographyusual attribute: intelligence untrained: limitedcar­to­graphy covers reading, copying, cor­rect­ing, and cre­at­ing maps. a car­to­grapher can inter­pret symbols and scale, compare con­flict­ing maps, trans­late meas­ure­ments and route notes into a usable rep­res­ent­a­tion, update a map after the land­scape has changed, and recog­nize when dis­tances, land­marks, or terrain do not fit together.anyone may sketch a famil­iar road or mark a remembered land­mark. pro­du­cing an accur­ate working map, repair­ing an incom­plete chart, or com­bin­ing several imper­fect accounts requires train­ing.car­to­graphy records what is known about the land. nav­ig­a­tion uses that inform­a­tion, together with obser­va­tion and remembered geo­graphy, to determ­ine pos­i­tion and course.

sections.title: Command
sections.text: commandusual attribute: charisma untrained: yescommand gives clear orders, assigns imme­di­ate respons­ib­il­it­ies, and keeps people working together when speed, danger, noise, or con­fu­sion could break their coordin­a­tion. it applies to a crew, patrol, work gang, nearby mil­it­ary unit, or similar group the char­ac­ter can per­son­ally direct.a com­mander might assign a patrol to several entrances, organ­ize workers around a col­lapsing struc­ture, call a deck crew to prepare for a squall, or restore order after con­flict­ing instruc­tions. the skill helps make pri­or­it­ies under­stood and keeps atten­tion on the shared task.command is per­sonal and imme­di­ate: the char­ac­ter must be able to com­mu­nic­ate with the group and observe the work closely enough to direct it. use mass combat when dir­ect­ing form­a­tions in battle and the ruler system when gov­ern­ing estates, armies, courts, fac­tions, or coun­tries.

sections.title: Commerce
sections.text: commerceusual attribute: intelligence untrained: yescom­merce is prac­tical know­ledge of markets, trade customs, con­tracts, supply, bar­gain­ing, and the move­ment of goods. it helps a char­ac­ter locate buyers or sellers, recog­nize scarcity or unusual prices, under­stand the terms of a trans­ac­tion, and judge how mer­chand­ise reaches a region.a mer­chant might identify the market most likely to accept foreign coin, dis­cover which caravan con­trols the local salt supply, nego­ti­ate a bulk pur­chase, or notice that a con­tract quietly trans­fers an unusual risk to the buyer. avail­able altern­at­ives, urgency, repu­ta­tion, and know­ledge of the market all shape the bargain.appraisal can estab­lish the work­man­ship and likely value of a jeweled cup. com­merce finds the buyer who wants it, pre­dicts what that buyer may pay, and nego­ti­ates the terms of sale.

sections.title: Craft (Field)
sections.text: craft (field)usual attribute: varies untrained: limitedcraft governs the prac­tical work of a learned trade, from select­ing mater­i­als and plan­ning the task through shaping, fitting, assem­bling, fin­ish­ing, and repair. each field is a sep­ar­ate skill.

sections.title: Cryptography
sections.text: cryptographyusual attribute: intelligence untrained: trained onlycryp­to­graphy covers recog­niz­ing, cre­at­ing, and deci­pher­ing delib­er­ate codes and ciphers. it exam­ines repeated symbols, sub­sti­tu­tions, pat­terns, keys, con­ven­tional open­ings, and the struc­ture of a message to under­stand how its con­tents have been con­cealed.a cryp­to­grapher might compare several inter­cep­ted mes­sages for a shared system, prepare a message using an estab­lished code, recog­nize that appar­ently ordin­ary writing con­tains an encoded pattern, or work from context and sur­viv­ing frag­ments to recon­struct a cipher.deci­pher­ing the code reveals the message as written; it does not grant fluency in its lan­guage. unfa­mil­iar lan­guages and scripts use lin­guist­ics or the rel­ev­ant know­ledge field.

sections.title: Diplomacy
sections.text: diplomacyusual attribute: charisma untrained: yesdip­lomacy per­suades, nego­ti­ates, medi­ates dis­putes, and presents terms in a form another person may accept. it can secure a hearing, request aid or access, improve strained rela­tions, broker an exchange, calm a dispute, or find a work­able com­prom­ise between com­pet­ing interests.

sections.title: Engineering
sections.text: engineeringusual attribute: intelligence untrained: trained onlyengin­eer­ing covers the design and ana­lysis of struc­tures, machines, for­ti­fic­a­tions, bridges, water­works, and com­par­able con­struc­ted systems. it con­siders sup­ports, loads, stresses, moving parts, mater­i­als, drain­age, and likely points of failure.a sagging bridge can be examined for failing sup­ports, a hoist judged against its inten­ded load, and a for­ti­fic­a­tion studied for vul­ner­able points. engin­eer­ing also plans the passage of water through a mill or set­tle­ment and tests whether a pro­posed alter­a­tion will weaken a larger struc­ture.engin­eer­ing sup­plies the design and tech­nical judg­ment. the rel­ev­ant craft carries out con­struc­tion, fitting, and repair.

sections.title: Escape Artist
sections.text: escape artistusual attribute: dexterity untrained: yesescape artist uses flex­ib­il­ity, lever­age, and careful move­ment to slip bonds, work free of a net or entangling wrap, squeeze through a con­fined opening, or release a trapped limb. a char­ac­ter might search for slack in tied wrists, turn the body through a gap barely large enough to permit passage, or free a boot caught between stones.the restraint must leave some plaus­ible room, weak­ness, or lever­age to exploit. opening a locked restraint calls for locks and traps.grapples always use the combat pro­ced­ure; escape artist never sub­sti­tutes for or assists that check.

sections.title: Etiquette
sections.text: etiquetteusual attribute: charisma untrained: yesetiquette is fluency in the manners, titles, cere­mon­ies, and expect­a­tions of struc­tured society. it helps a char­ac­ter choose the proper form of address, make intro­duc­tions, exchange gifts, observe pre­ced­ence, dress for an occa­sion, and move through formal gath­er­ings without cre­at­ing an unin­ten­ded insult.the skill can also reveal meaning carried through cere­mony. a change in seating may signal favor or dis­grace; an omitted title may be a care­less mistake or a delib­er­ate slight; an unusu­ally valu­able gift may create an expect­a­tion that nobody states aloud.famil­iar customs are usually straight­for­ward. foreign courts, obscure rites, old mil­it­ary tra­di­tions, and cere­mon­ies designed to test an out­sider may be con­sid­er­ably harder to nav­ig­ate.skill mastery: etiquetteetiquette skill mastery allows a char­ac­ter to design a complex cere­mony, formal recep­tion, or order of pre­ced­ence that brings several known tra­di­tions together without cre­at­ing unin­ten­ded insults or con­tra­dic­tions.the char­ac­ter must first under­stand the customs being incor­por­ated. a rel­ev­ant know­ledge skill may be needed for an unfa­mil­iar faith, court, mil­it­ary tra­di­tion, or culture.etiquette determ­ines the correct forms, honors, and cere­mo­nial arrange­ment. dip­lomacy remains respons­ible for nego­ti­at­ing accept­ance, resolv­ing oppos­i­tion, and per­suad­ing par­ti­cipants to cooper­ate.

sections.title: Forgery
sections.text: forgeryusual attribute: dexterity untrained: limitedforgery is used to create or alter doc­u­ments, imitate hand­writ­ing, repro­duce seals, and falsify records. it can change a name, date, amount, or author­iz­a­tion; create a pass or letter from a suit­able example; insert a plaus­ible entry into a ledger; or repro­duce the visible marks by which an insti­tu­tion recog­nizes its doc­u­ments.the same train­ing helps examine sus­pi­cious writing. a prac­ticed forger may recog­nize incon­sist­ent strokes, an incor­rectly repro­duced seal, an alter­a­tion con­cealed beneath later work, or methods famil­iar from other false doc­u­ments.basic alter­a­tions may be attemp­ted untrained. con­vin­cing offi­cial records, unfa­mil­iar scripts, closely con­trolled seals, and other tech­nical work require train­ing, suit­able examples, and appro­pri­ate mater­i­als. phys­ical coun­ter­feits such as coins use the rel­ev­ant craft.skill mastery: forgeryforgery skill mastery allows a char­ac­ter to create a con­nec­ted body of false records whose dates, ref­er­ences, author­it­ies, sig­na­tures, seals, and entries support one another. this can estab­lish a con­vin­cing paper trail across several doc­u­ments rather than relying on a single isol­ated false­hood.the attempt requires suit­able mater­i­als and enough genuine examples to repro­duce the insti­tu­tion's forms and identi­fy­ing marks.research may be needed to dis­cover the records, pro­ced­ures, names, and past events with which the false doc­u­ments must agree. forgery creates and alters the doc­u­ments them­selves; phys­ical coun­ter­feits such as coins remain the work of the rel­ev­ant craft.

sections.title: Gaming
sections.text: gamingusual attribute: intelligence untrained: yesgaming covers the rules, cus­tom­ary play, strategy, odds, and table con­ven­tions of games of chance or skill. it helps a char­ac­ter judge a pos­i­tion, choose sound play, recog­nize an exper­i­enced oppon­ent, assess risk, and learn an unfa­mil­iar game through obser­va­tion and explan­a­tion.during play, gaming may reveal that an oppon­ent is setting up a famil­iar strategy, that a wager is poor for the appar­ent odds, or that a local rule changes the value of an oth­er­wise strong move. it also helps dis­tin­guish ordin­ary custom from beha­vior that should draw sus­pi­cion.a cheater may use bluff to mislead oppon­ents or sleight of hand to manip­u­late cards, dice, or pieces. gaming sup­plies the under­stand­ing needed to choose a useful decep­tion and recog­nize the risks involved.

sections.title: Golem Piloting
sections.text: golem pilotingusual attribute: dexterity  untrained: limitedgolem pilot­ing governs oper­a­tion of an elven-inter­face golem frame: delib­er­ate loco­motion, dif­fi­cult terrain, close man­euv­er­ing, jumps, falls, forced move­ment, unstable footing, damaged con­trols, melee hand­ling, and active defens­ive hand­ling.routine walking, turning, and com­par­able oper­a­tion need no check for a qual­i­fied pilot. when an uncer­tain con­sequen­tial task requires a check, use the com­plete ordin­ary skill pro­ced­ure. untrained use is limited to the expli­cit emer­gency-oper­a­tion pro­ced­ure; it does not make the oper­ator a qual­i­fied pilot.frame combat also derives a small flat pilot­ing com­pet­ence mod­i­fier from the gov­ern­ing golem pilot­ing attrib­ute. that mod­i­fier is not the pilot's skill threshold and is used only where the golem frames rules expressly call for it.

sections.title: Golem Senses
sections.text: golem sensesusual attribute: wisdom  untrained: yes — requires training in golem pilotinggolem senses governs inter­pret­a­tion of a frame's sensory feed: peri­pheral threats, rapidly chan­ging pos­i­tions, com­mu­nic­a­tions, damaged sensors, poor vis­ib­il­ity, and inform­a­tion over­load.a char­ac­ter trained in golem pilot­ing may attempt golem senses untrained. begin with half wisdom, rounded down, then apply the normal dif­fi­culty, frame

sections.title: Investigation
sections.text: investigationusual attribute: intelligence untrained: yesinvest­ig­a­tion covers delib­er­ate exam­in­a­tion of a place, object, account, or chain of events. it searches for rel­ev­ant traces, com­pares state­ments with phys­ical evid­ence, tests pos­sible explan­a­tions, recog­nizes con­nec­tions, and recon­structs what most likely happened.a char­ac­ter might determ­ine how someone entered a locked room, estab­lish which damage occurred first, notice that a scene was rearranged, compare several wit­nesses' accounts, or connect an appar­ently ordin­ary object to an earlier event. incom­plete, damaged, or delib­er­ately mis­lead­ing evid­ence may support only a partial con­clu­sion.per­cep­tion might reveal fresh mud beneath a window. invest­ig­a­tion con­nects it to the forced latch and the foot­prints outside. research can then follow a maker's mark or own­er­ship record through an archive.

sections.title: Intimidation
sections.text: intimidationusual attribute: charisma untrained: yesintim­id­a­tion pres­sures another person toward hes­it­a­tion, com­pli­ance, retreat, silence, or dis­clos­ure through menace, author­ity, fear, or a cred­ible threat. it can make a bel­li­ger­ent stranger recon­sider a fight, compel a tres­passer to leave, silence delib­er­ate dis­rup­tion, or press a frightened captive for an answer.the target's courage, oblig­a­tions, avail­able altern­at­ives, and belief in the threat shape both the dif­fi­culty and the response. intim­id­a­tion remains con­vin­cing while the danger and the char­ac­ter's ability to carry it out remain cred­ible.

sections.title: Knowledge (Field)
sections.text: knowledge (field)usual attribute: intelligence untrained: trained onlyknow­ledge covers learned inform­a­tion within a par­tic­u­lar field. each field is a sep­ar­ate skill. a check may recall a fact, recog­nize a person, place, object, prac­tice, or phe­nomenon con­nec­ted to the subject, inter­pret evid­ence through that dis­cip­line, explain its sig­ni­fic­ance, or connect several pieces of learned inform­a­tion.common inform­a­tion that requires no spe­cial­ist edu­ca­tion may use an ordin­ary intel­li­gence check. a trained-only know­ledge check applies when the ques­tion depends on study within the named field.the obscur­ity, age, loc­al­ity, and spe­cial­ist nature of the inform­a­tion shape the dif­fi­culty. know­ledge (her­aldry) might identify a house from a damaged badge, know­ledge (geology) might explain an unusual seam in a cavern wall, and know­ledge (reli­gion) might place an unfa­mil­iar rite within a known faith.use the single best-fitting know­ledge skill for one ques­tion. broad and narrow fields do not stack and do not provide several attempts at the same fact. spe­cificity changes dif­fi­culty: an obscure tasla­maran geo­graph­ical fact may be extreme for know­ledge (geo­graphy) and easy or normal for know­ledge (tasla­maran geo­graphy).natural world and places: anatomy; botany; creatures (a spe­cific family); geo­graphy; geology; local know­ledge (a spe­cific place); nature.history and society: ancient history; archae­ology and ruins; her­aldry; history; law; nobil­ity and gene­a­logy; polit­ics; tactics; under­world.thought, belief, and lan­guage: astro­logy; folk­lore; know­ledge (lan­guage: spe­cific lan­guage); occult; philo­sophy; reli­gion; spirits; theo­logy.tech­nical and magical study: astro­nomy; magic; math­em­at­ics; metal­lurgy; planes and cos­mo­logy; spell­craft.know­ledge (magic) covers broad magical schol­ar­ship: magical tra­di­tions, com­monly recog­nized spells, magical creatures, objects, phe­nom­ena, and general theory.know­ledge (spell­craft) studies how spells are con­struc­ted and operate. it can identify a spell as it is cast, decipher another caster's research, and analyze active

sections.title: Linguistics
sections.text: linguisticsusual attribute: intelligence untrained: trained onlylin­guist­ics is the com­par­at­ive study of lan­guage, scripts, dia­lects, trans­la­tion, ety­mo­logy, and accents. it can identify the family or region from which a lan­guage developed, dis­tin­guish closely related dia­lects, recog­nize bor­rowed words, compare dif­fer­ent ver­sions of a text, and explain what an accent or unusual con­struc­tion sug­gests about a speaker or writer.the skill also helps trans­late unfa­mil­iar or archaic pas­sages when related lan­guages and suf­fi­cient context provide a basis for com­par­ison. a lin­guist may recon­struct missing words from grammar, recover part of a damaged inscrip­tion, or determ­ine how a term's meaning changed between periods, although the sur­viv­ing evid­ence may limit the cer­tainty or com­plete­ness of the reading.fluency in a par­tic­u­lar lan­guage comes from its spe­cific know­ledge field. delib­er­ate codes and ciphers use cryp­to­graphy.skill mastery: linguisticsgiven a sub­stan­tial body of related sur­viv­ing texts and enough time to compare them, a char­ac­ter with lin­guist­ics skill mastery may attempt to recon­struct a pro­vi­sional grammar and lexicon for an unknown or dead lan­guage. the recon­struc­tion provides a basis for later lin­guist­ics checks to trans­late pas­sages sup­por­ted by that evid­ence.its con­clu­sions are limited by the sur­viv­ing texts and cannot supply missing vocab­u­lary, grammar, or meaning for which no evid­ence exists.this recon­struc­tion grants neither con­ver­sa­tional nor routine reading fluency; fluency still requires the appro­pri­ate know­ledge (lan­guage: spe­cific lan­guage) skill. delib­er­ate codes and ciphers remain the province of cryp­to­graphy.

sections.title: Locks and Traps
sections.text: locks and trapsusual attribute: dexterity untrained: limitedlocks and traps covers examin­ing, opening, bypassing, dis­arm­ing, and reset­ting mech­an­ical locks and traps. it allows a char­ac­ter to under­stand how a mech­an­ism is arranged, identify the part that holds or releases it, and manip­u­late its com­pon­ents without relying on force alone.

sections.title: Medicine
sections.text: medicineusual attribute: wisdom untrained: limitedmedi­cine governs dia­gnosis, pro­gnosis, con­tinu­ing care, pre­ven­tion, and ordin­ary treat­ment. a trained char­ac­ter can examine symp­toms and injur­ies, judge their sever­ity and likely pro­gres­sion, choose appro­pri­ate mundane care, and monitor whether a patient is recov­er­ing as expec­ted.its ordin­ary prac­tice includes clean­ing and dress­ing injur­ies, recog­niz­ing signs of disease or poison, setting rest and san­it­a­tion require­ments, select­ing a suit­able diet or medi­cine, determ­in­ing a safe dose, and adjust­ing care when a patient's con­di­tion changes.an untrained char­ac­ter may recog­nize obvious dis­tress, provide simple care, or follow instruc­tions from a trained care­giver. tech­nical dia­gnosis, com­plic­ated treat­ment, and pro­fes­sional con­tinu­ing care require train­ing.

sections.title: Navigation
sections.text: navigationusual attribute: intelligence untrained: limitednav­ig­a­tion determ­ines pos­i­tion, chooses a route, and keeps a journey on course by using land­marks, maps, stars, instru­ments, or remembered geo­graphy. on land, it may compare visible terrain with a map, choose between known roads or cross­ings, retrace a route, or main­tain dir­ec­tion where no road exists. at sea, it may estab­lish pos­i­tion, account for drift, and plot a course from obser­va­tions.an untrained char­ac­ter may follow obvious land­marks or a clearly marked route. uncer­tain pos­i­tion, poor vis­ib­il­ity, open water, and other tech­nical or haz­ard­ous nav­ig­a­tion require train­ing.aboard a vessel, the nav­ig­ator plots and main­tains the course from maps and obser­va­tions; the crew uses seaman­ship to carry out the needed changes in sail and helm.

sections.title: Perception
