pages.title: Warlock · Starting Package
pages.text: classeswarlock70classes · warlockwarlockidentity and role. warlocks inherit or awaken an affinity with elemental powers, often through an ancestral bargain or altered bloodline. their elementalism favors direct offense and defense, elemental conjuration, and summoning, and their training prepares them to cast amid close danger. training teaches control and combat use but cannot ordinarily create the affinity. a character may begin with warlock when that relationship is part of the character; taking the job later requires the affinity to be established and follows the ordinary additional-job training procedure.progression. warlocks use shared advancement and the mage chassis above. a warlock's ordinary armed and unarmed attack speed is 1 unless an explicit talent, weapon configuration, spell, or other rule changes it.starting packageequipment training. acquiring warlock job level 1 ordinarily grants training with dagger, flail, mace, sling, crossbow, and unarmed combat, together with light armor. it grants no staff weapon, shield, medium-armor, or heavy-armor training. culturally restricted, specialist, and item-specific equipment still requires its own training.casting in light armor. a warlock may cast warlock spells in trained light armor without that armor's spell failure. mobility and every other armor penalty still apply. this permission does not apply to a shield, medium or heavy armor, untrained armor, or a spell from another job unless an explicit rule says otherwise.apprentice talent access. wands, staves, and scrolls become available for purchase. none is learned automatically.class talentsthe rank table below lists every talent available through the warlock job. complete descriptions and xp costs for these generic talents appear in talents and feats. the notes below distinguish similarly named weapon and device training.warlock ranktalent accessapprenticewands; staves; scrollsjourneymanself defenseveterantrance; enduranceexpertbrew; lucid dreamingmentorscribe; claritymastertrackingwands, staves, and scrolls are separate device talents. staves does not grant staff weapon training, and neither of the other device talents accompanies it. tracking remains a generic purchased talent rather than a special elemental procedure. metamagic is absent from this purchased ladder because the mage chassis grants its selections automatically.warlock has no class mastery. warlock spells, metamagic, ritual spell eligibility, light-armor casting permission, and talents remain available during a round in which the character uses another job's class mastery, unless an ability says otherwise.warlock spellcastingwarlock caster level equals half warlock job level, rounded down. warlock spells use the character's one me pool and the ordinary spell dc.warlocks use a curated elementalism spell list. the catalogue, general spell-learning procedure, spell descriptions, device interactions, individual metamagic abilities, ritual spell boundary, and individual rituals appear in spells and spellcasting. job level supplies circle eligibility rather than automatic spell knowledge.

pages.title: Spell Access · Example: Armor training and magical devices
pages.text: classeswarlock71classes · warlockspell accessjob level is the access requirement rather than caster level. each spell must also appear on the curated warlock list and satisfy its learning requirements.warlock job levelhighest spell circle1-4none5-617-829-11312-14415-17518-21622-25726-29830-319first-circle access begins at warlock job level 5. the warlock's caster level is 2 at that point.example: armor training and magical devicesa warlock wearing trained light armor may cast a learned warlock spell without rolling that armor's spell failure. the armor's mobility and every other penalty still apply. the same permission does not protect a spell granted by another job, and it does not extend to medium armor merely because the warlock has somehow become trained with it.if the warlock purchases staves, the character may use magical staves under the device rules in spells and spellcasting. this does not train the warlock to wield staff as a weapon. it also grants neither wands nor scrolls; each device talent must be purchased separately.related rulestalents and feats gives xp costs and complete rules for wands, staves, scrolls, self defense, trance, endurance, brew, lucid dreaming, scribe, clarity, and tracking. the elementalism spell list, spell-learning rules, spell descriptions, device interactions, individual metamagic abilities, and ritual spells appear in spells and spellcasting.

pages.title: Necromancer · Starting Package
pages.text: classesnecromancer72classes · necromancernecromanceridentity and role. necromancers are mages whose magic has been claimed and translated by the abyss, where dead realities, destroyed concepts, and impossible things persist outside ordinary existence. their power can force effects reality would not ordinarily permit, and the relationship remains corrupting regardless of the practitioner's intent.necromancer is a restricted job that requires explicit dm permission and an appropriate campaign. it is not an ordinary starting choice. a person may be forced or drawn into necromancy through an initiation, ritual, or artifact; prior mage training is not required. because a character may possess only one mage job, becoming a necromancer converts an existing sorcerer or warlock job in place rather than adding another mage job. a character without a mage job instead acquires necromancer at job level 1 through the ordinary additional-job procedure.progression. necromancers use shared advancement and the mage chassis above. a necromancer's ordinary armed and unarmed attack speed is 1 unless an explicit talent, weapon configuration, spell, or other rule changes it.starting packagethis package applies only to a character who acquires necromancer without converting an existing mage job. a conversion preserves the former job's history and grants none of these level-1 benefits a second time.equipment training. acquiring necromancer at job level 1 grants training with dagger, staff, sling, crossbow, and unarmed combat. it grants no armor or shield training and no permission to ignore armor spell failure. culturally restricted, specialist, and item-specific equipment still requires its own training.apprentice talent access. wands, staves, and scrolls become available for purchase. none is learned automatically.class talentsthe rank table below lists every talent available through the necromancer job. complete descriptions and xp costs for these generic talents appear in talents and feats. the special necromancer procedures that follow remain complete in this profile.necromancer ranktalent accessapprenticewands; staves; scrollsjourneymanself defenseveterantranceexpertbrew; scribe; lucid dreamingmentorclaritymasterno additional talentwands, staves, and scrolls are separate talents. brew and scribe follow the general talent rules in talents and feats. no additional talent becomes available at master rank. metamagic is absent from this purchased ladder because the mage chassis grants its selections automatically. ritual spell eligibility grants no ritual automatically and remains distinct from true necromancy.necromancer has no class mastery. necromancer spells, true necromancy, metamagic, ritual spell eligibility, and ordinary or legacy talents remain available during a round in which the character uses another job's class mastery, unless an ability says otherwise.necromancer spellcastingnecromancer caster level equals half necromancer job level, rounded down. necromancer spells use the character's one me pool and the ordinary spell dc. necromancers use a curated spell list, which appears in spells and spellcasting. job level supplies circle eligibility rather than automatic spell knowledge.

pages.title: Spell Access · Corrupted Magic
pages.text: classesnecromancer73classes · necromancerspell accesseach spell learned through necromancer job access must appear on the necromancer list and satisfy its learning requirements. another explicit rule may grant its own access.necromancer job levelhighest spell circle1-4none5-617-829-11312-14415-17518-21622-25726-29830-319first-circle access begins at necromancer job level 5, when the necromancer's caster level is 2. first-circle access also unlocks true necromancy.corrupted magicevery magical effect the necromancer personally invokes becomes abyssal and necromantic in source, manifestation, detection, descriptors, and supernatural interaction. unless an effect says otherwise, its numerical result remains unchanged. this translation does not grant access to a spell or device the character could not otherwise use and does not waive an effect's ordinary action, cost, or requirements.translated spells resolve according to their usual rules. they do not invoke true necromancy merely because their source and appearance have become abyssal.the corruption rejects unconverted non-abyssal magical energy and makes attempts to channel it painful. when this rejection matters, resolve its harm according to the effect's rules or the dm's ruling.

pages.title: True Necromancy · Dark Points
pages.text: classesnecromancer74classes · necromancertrue necromancytrue necromancy is a freeform abyssal working rather than an ordinary fixed spell. it becomes available when the necromancer gains first-circle spell access. a working can be a prepared ritual lasting hours or days, a repeatable ritual already settled with the dm, or an improvised plea attempted with a main action.the necromancer states the desired result, wording, casting time, preparation, and deliberate offerings. an offering may be a life, goods, a relationship, or another sacrifice whose loss has genuine value to the people involved. the dm judges that value and whether it is proportionate to the request; there is no universal price table.the dm assigns an equivalent spell circle from the working's scope. the necromancer's highest accessible circle is the expected scope, not an absolute prohibition: an attempt beyond it may be allowed with dramatically worse and potentially undisclosed odds or terms. a working beyond the ordinary spell scale remains wholly dm-adjudicated and gains no automatic higher circle.dark points measure accumulated personal corruption on a scale from 0 to 10. the control roll below may add them; their complete consequences and recovery appear under dark points.resolve the working in this order:set control chance. it begins at the necromancer's charisma score as a percentage. the dm adjusts it for scope, preparation, wording, casting time, offerings, and circumstances, and need not disclose the final number.roll control. roll d100. a result equal to or below the control chance keeps the working under the necromancer's control and adds no dark point. on a higher result, the abyss may distort, overfulfill, or exact another price. the dm determines the outcome and whether the necromancer gains any dark points and, if so, how many.consume offerings. offerings are consumed regardless of the control result and are not returned by later complications.check world rejection. when the counter force can perceive the working, roll d10. if the result is equal to or below the equivalent spell circle, roll d20 for severity and let the dm determine how reality suppresses, redirects, exposes, or complicates the working.control and world rejection are independent. a controlled working can still be rejected, and an uncontrolled working can escape notice. offerings remain consumed and dark points remain gained even when world rejection prevents the intended result.being inside a reality marble does not by itself conceal the working from the counter force or exempt it from world rejection. apply the same perception condition and check. any protective or concealing effect depends on a specific established mechanism. the marble's own rules may additionally prohibit, alter, or punish necromancy. control, offerings, dark points, and abyssal consequences continue to apply.dark pointswhenever a resolution raises the dark point total to 4 or higher, roll d10. if the result is equal to or below the current dark points, the abyss claims the character; the character becomes unplayable and passes to the dm. a total of 10 guarantees this result.dark points can fade through prolonged abstinence from necromancy. because all magic personally invoked by a necromancer is translated into abyssal necromancy, ordinary translated spells also interrupt the interval:current dark pointsordinary interval before a recovery roll1about one month2about six months3about one to two years4 or morean increasingly long interval set by the dmwhen the interval passes without the necromancer personally invoking any necromancy, roll d10. a result greater than the current dark points removes one point. any other result removes none, and another full interval must pass before trying again.

pages.title: Converting an Existing Mage Job · Example: A Warlock becoming a Necromancer
pages.text: classesnecromancer75classes · necromancerconverting an existing mage jobwhen sorcerer or warlock becomes necromancer, convert that job in place:preserve its job level, rank, job xp, acquisition order, main- or secondary-job status, and tie precedence. do not charge another job-entry cost.preserve overall-level history, purchased bab, saving throws, advancement trains, pe, me, current and maximum me, and every earlier mage-chassis benefit. recalculate only values normally derived from the renamed job, such as the displayed job name and caster level. conversion grants no refill, refund, backfill, duplicate chassis benefit, or free train reselection.preserve learned metamagic abilities and ritual spells. conversion grants no additional selection and no free reselection.preserve every spell actually learned as a legacy spell. it becomes necromantic when the character invokes it. the former job's spell list closes for future learning; new spells must come from the necromancer list or another explicit source.preserve purchased generic talents, but close the former job's access ladder for future purchases. a purchased sorcerer arcane ward or mana shield remains as a legacy talent and becomes necromantic when used; neither enters the necromancer ladder. when the converted necromancer uses either retained talent, references to the sorcerer in its procedure mean that converted character; every other part of the procedure remains unchanged.preserve mundane equipment training. do not grant the necromancer level-1 equipment package during conversion. former job-specific magical permissions end unless this profile explicitly preserves them; warlock's trained-light-armor spell failure waiver therefore ends.conversion is ordinarily one-way. reversing it requires an exceptional dm-approved event and is not ordinary retraining or job switching.example: a warlock becoming a necromancera level-12 warlock is converted in place. the character becomes a level-12 necromancer, retaining the same job xp, rank, acquisition order, main- or secondary-job status, and tie precedence. caster level remains 6, and job level 12 still permits spell access through fourth circle.the character keeps purchased bab and saves, advancement trains, pe, current and maximum me, every earned mage-chassis benefit, learned metamagic abilities, ritual spells, purchased talents, and mundane equipment training. learned warlock spells remain as legacy spells and become necromantic when invoked. the former warlock spell list and talent ladder no longer grant future choices; new spells and talent purchases must use necromancer access or another explicit source.the conversion grants no necromancer starting package, me refill, refund, backfill, additional metamagic selection, or free reselection. light-armor training remains, but the warlock-only spell failure waiver ends, so the armor's listed spell failure applies when the character casts necromancer spells.related rulestrue necromancy and mage-job conversion use the complete procedures above. talents and feats gives xp costs and complete rules for the purchased generic talents. the necromancer spell list, spell descriptions and learning, device interactions, individual metamagic abilities, ritual spells, and detailed legacy-spell adaptation appear in spells and spellcasting.

pages.title: Using Skills · Attribute Checks and Skill Checks
pages.text: skillsusing skillsusing skillsattribute checks and skill checksmost ordin­ary activ­ity needs no roll. make a check when the result is genu­inely uncer­tain and success or failure matters.an attrib­ute check resolves some­thing a plaus­ible char­ac­ter could attempt without a named body of train­ing. roll d20 equal to or below the rel­ev­ant raw attrib­ute score after apply­ing dif­fi­culty and other mod­i­fi­ers.a skill check resolves a task gov­erned by a named skill. a trained char­ac­ter begins with the full rel­ev­ant attrib­ute score. a char­ac­ter who lacks the skill follows its untrained rule; the same task does not become an attrib­ute check merely because the untrained threshold is less favor­able.a short, ordin­ary jump may call for a dex­ter­ity check. a dif­fi­cult leap that requires trained body control may call for acro­bat­ics instead.choosing the governing attributeeach skill lists its usual attrib­ute, which is the normal start­ing point for its checks. the dm may choose another attrib­ute when the char­ac­ter genu­inely uses a dif­fer­ent method.intim­id­a­tion ordin­ar­ily uses cha­risma when the char­ac­ter relies on pres­ence, threats, or force of per­son­al­ity. a display of phys­ical menace may use strength instead. the skill remains intim­id­a­tion; only the attrib­ute gov­ern­ing that attempt changes.trained and untrained usea trained skill check begins with the full gov­ern­ing attrib­ute. an untrained attempt that the skill permits begins with half the gov­ern­ing attrib­ute, rounded down. apply dif­fi­culty and other mod­i­fi­ers after estab­lish­ing that start­ing threshold.the untrained line in each skill entry uses one of three labels:untrained meaning yes ordinary uses may be attempted untrained. limited basic or obvious uses may be attempted untrained. technical, professional, or hazardous uses require training. trained only the named skill use requires training. an ordinary nontechnical action may still be an attribute check when it does not require that body of knowledge. for example, a char­ac­ter with dex­ter­ity 15 begins a trained acro­bat­ics check at 15. if the attemp­ted use permits an untrained check, the char­ac­ter instead begins at 7 after round­ing down. normal dif­fi­culty lowers that untrained threshold to 5.difficultyafter estab­lish­ing the check's start­ing threshold, apply the task's dif­fi­culty:difficulty easy normal hard very hard extreme modifier — -2 -4 -6 -8 easy rep­res­ents a mean­ing­ful check under favor­able or ordin­ary cir­cum­stances. normal intro­duces some risk or com­plic­a­tion. hard, very hard, and extreme rep­res­ent increas­ingly demand­ing cir­cum­stances, with extreme forming the prac­tical end of the ordin­ary ladder. a spe­cific skill, talent, spell, or other rule may state another mod­i­fier when its own pro­ced­ure requires one.bonuses raise the threshold; pen­al­ties and dif­fi­culty lower it. roll d20. a result equal to or below the final threshold suc­ceeds. natural 1 and natural 20 have no sep­ar­ate auto­matic effect on a roll-under check; compare the result with the threshold nor­mally. an unmod­i­fied threshold of 20 cannot fail an ordin­ary d20 check.76skills · using skills

pages.title: Using Skills · continued · Opposed Checks and Check Margin
pages.text: skillsusing skillsusing skills · continuedopposed checks and check marginwhen two char­ac­ters dir­ectly oppose one another, both make the required check. for each par­ti­cipant, sub­tract the d20 result from the adjus­ted threshold. the result is the char­ac­ter's check margin.the higher check margin wins, even when both margins are neg­at­ive. a tie favors the defender. check margin is sep­ar­ate from an attack's margin of success.when a rule says that an opposed check suc­ceeds by 8 or more, the winning check margin must exceed the losing margin by at least 8. in an unop­posed check, failure by 8 or more means a check margin of -8 or lower.example: opposed check marginsone par­ti­cipant has an adjus­ted threshold of 20 and rolls 23, pro­du­cing a check margin of -3. the other has a threshold of 18 and rolls 20, pro­du­cing a check margin of -2. both rolled above their thresholds, but -2 is the higher margin, so the second par­ti­cipant wins. if both margins were equal, the defender would win.time, attempts, and repeated efforta check takes however long the attemp­ted task nat­ur­ally requires. a spe­cific skill use, talent, combat option, or other rule states an exact action or dur­a­tion when timing matters.one roll ordin­ar­ily rep­res­ents the com­plete attempt. failure does not grant unlim­ited con­sequence-free rerolls through the same method. another attempt becomes pos­sible when the task nat­ur­ally permits repeated effort, but each attempt con­sumes its normal time and carries the cir­cum­stances and con­sequences of con­tinu­ing.a char­ac­ter may keep trying to force a door, for example, while every attempt takes time and makes noise. research­ing the same exhausted source again does not produce another answer unless the char­ac­ter brings new inform­a­tion, gains access to dif­fer­ent mater­ial, or changes the method.skills and talentsskills describe learned, repeat­able com­pet­en­cies. talents grant excep­tional train­ing or abil­it­ies that may use, improve, replace, or auto­mat­ic­ally resolve a skill check.stealth remains the ordin­ary skill behind con­ceal­ment and quiet move­ment; hide and sneak provide their own excep­tional bene­fits. sur­vival sup­ports delib­er­ate exam­in­a­tion of tracks; the track­ing talent permits much faster recog­ni­tion and pursuit of usable signs. medi­cine covers dia­gnosis and con­tinu­ing care; field medic provides urgent treat­ment under field pres­sure.when a talent changes a skill, use the talent's com­plete rule. learn­ing the skill alone does not grant the talent, and learn­ing the talent does not trans­form it into a second skill.77skills · using skills

pages.title: Learning Skills and Skill Mastery · Starting Skills
pages.text: skillslearning skills · skill cataloguelearning skills and skill masterystarting skillsa new char­ac­ter receives start­ing skills in three parts:choose three skills appro­pri­ate to the train­ing of the char­ac­ter's start­ing job. choose from the full skill cata­logue, subject to dm approval.add unres­tric­ted skill choices equal to the char­ac­ter's pos­it­ive per­man­ent intel­li­gence mod­i­fier after racial and prime-attrib­ute adjust­ments. a mod­i­fier of +0 or lower adds no choices and never removes any of the three job-based choices.a human adds one further unres­tric­ted skill choice.a repeated choice must be replaced rather than learned twice. each sep­ar­ately named craft, know­ledge, per­form­ance, or pro­fes­sion field is a sep­ar­ate skill. know­ledge (history) and know­ledge (lan­guage: ayamaoan), for example, are two dif­fer­ent choices.lan­guages granted by region, race, or a start­ing mage job cost no start­ing skill choices; char­ac­ter cre­ation lists those grants. every addi­tional lan­guage is its own know­ledge (lan­guage: spe­cific lan­guage) skill and uses one start­ing skill choice unless another rule grants it. learn­ing a special lan­guage during cre­ation requires dm per­mis­sion and appro­pri­ate access.start­ing skill choices grant trained skills, not skill mas­ter­ies. intel­li­gence determ­ines how many skill mas­ter­ies the char­ac­ter may even­tu­ally know; it does not grant those mas­ter­ies auto­mat­ic­ally. acquir­ing another job later does not repeat these cre­ation-only choices.learning a new skilllearn­ing a new skill after char­ac­ter cre­ation nor­mally costs 10 xp. the dm may raise the cost as high as 30 xp accord­ing to how dif­fi­cult or unfa­mil­iar that train­ing is for the char­ac­ter and the cir­cum­stances in which it is being learned.the char­ac­ter's exist­ing jobs, back­ground, exper­i­ence, access to inform­a­tion, and oppor­tun­ity to prac­tice all matter. a sor­cerer accus­tomed to lib­rar­ies and magical study may find sur­vival unusu­ally dif­fi­cult, while a career warrior may have the same dif­fi­culty learn­ing know­ledge (magic). this is a judg­ment made for the char­ac­ter and situ­ation, not a fixed com­pat­ib­il­ity table.a suit­able instructor may halve the final xp cost, to a minimum of 5 xp.skill masterya skill mastery unlocks the advanced uses described in that skill's mastery inset. it grants no uni­ver­sal numer­ical bonus and never guar­an­tees success. when the outcome remains uncer­tain, roll the under­ly­ing skill nor­mally.a char­ac­ter must know a skill before learn­ing its mastery, and the mastery must be learned or pur­chased; it is never gained auto­mat­ic­ally. each skill's mastery can be learned only once and never stacks with itself.the number of skill mas­ter­ies a char­ac­ter may know cannot exceed the char­ac­ter's per­man­ent intel­li­gence mod­i­fier, with a minimum capa­city of one. tem­por­ary effects and equip­ment do not create addi­tional capa­city.learn­ing a skill mastery takes at least six months and ordin­ar­ily takes about one year. it requires proper tutel­age: a qual­i­fied teacher, a uni­ver­sity or com­par­able insti­tu­tion, or another source capable of provid­ing sus­tained advanced train­ing.a skill mastery costs between 10 and 30 xp, as determ­ined by the dm accord­ing to the field, the avail­able tutel­age, and the cir­cum­stances of the train­ing.reading a skill entryeach entry begins with the skill's usual attrib­ute and its untrained label. the usual attrib­ute governs most attempts, although a genu­inely dif­fer­ent method may call for another attrib­ute. the untrained label states whether a char­ac­ter without the skill may attempt all ordin­ary uses, only basic uses, or none of the named skill uses.the descrip­tion iden­ti­fies the tasks the skill com­monly governs. a related talent line appears when a con­firmed talent builds on that skill and helps the reader find the excep­tional pro­ced­ure. a skill mastery section appears only when that skill has a com­plete advanced-use rule.78skills · learning skills · reading a skill entry

pages.title: Skill Catalogue · Acrobatics
pages.text: skillslearning skills · skill catalogueskill catalogueacrobaticsusual attribute: dexterity untrained: yesacro­bat­ics covers demand­ing move­ment that depends on balance, coordin­a­tion, and precise control. a char­ac­ter might use it to cross a narrow beam or rain-slick roof, keep footing on a swaying bridge, nego­ti­ate loose rubble, land under control after a dif­fi­cult drop, or place the body pre­cisely during a dif­fi­cult leap.use ath­let­ics when height, dis­tance, force, or sus­tained exer­tion is the central chal­lenge. acro­bat­ics applies when balance, place­ment, or a con­trolled landing matters most.related talent: tum­bling. tum­bling builds on acro­bat­ics for excep­tional move­ment.animal handlingusual attribute: wisdom untrained: yesanimal hand­ling governs imme­di­ate inter­ac­tion with an animal and the ability to read its present beha­vior. it may help a char­ac­ter approach a nervous horse, settle a pack animal frightened by noise or blood, lead live­stock through a crowded place, restrain an agit­ated dog, or recog­nize signs of fear, pain, aggres­sion, or exhaus­tion.the animal's tem­pera­ment, famili­ar­ity with the char­ac­ter, treat­ment, sur­round­ings, and current dis­tress shape the attempt. teach­ing lasting com­mands and prac­ticed beha­vior uses animal train­ing. when someone is already in the saddle, ride governs the rider's control while animal hand­ling remains rel­ev­ant when the animal's dis­pos­i­tion is the real dif­fi­culty.animal trainingusual attribute: wisdom untrained: limitedanimal train­ing teaches lasting com­mands, estab­lishes routines, and accus­toms an animal to unfa­mil­iar demands. it can teach an animal to halt, return, carry a rider or load, accept harness, remain man­age­able around crowds or loud activ­ity, and perform work appro­pri­ate to its nature and train­ing.train­ing takes the time appro­pri­ate to the animal and the beha­vior being taught. tem­pera­ment, prior treat­ment, danger, and the com­plex­ity of the desired beha­vior shape the task.animal training · continuedan untrained char­ac­ter may rein­force a simple beha­vior in a calm, famil­iar animal. dan­ger­ous animals and demand­ing or pro­fes­sional work require the skill. imme­di­ate attempts to calm, lead, or restrain an animal use animal hand­ling.skill mastery: animal traininganimal train­ing skill mastery unlocks complex train­ing. a char­ac­ter with this mastery can teach an animal linked routines made up of several famil­iar actions, rehab­il­it­ate entrenched fear or hos­til­ity caused by prior treat­ment, and train unusual animals that remain nat­ur­ally capable of learn­ing the desired beha­vior.the animal's nature and intel­li­gence still limit what it can learn, and train­ing still requires suit­able treat­ment, con­di­tions, and time.this mastery does not charm an animal, create super­nat­ural loyalty or an animal com­pan­ion, or grant the tame talent. it does not make an animal combat trained; the normal require­ments for combat train­ing still apply.appraisalusual attribute: intelligence untrained: limitedappraisal estim­ates an object's quality, con­di­tion, work­man­ship, authen­ti­city, and likely value. it can dis­tin­guish careful crafts­man­ship from dec­or­at­ive show, recog­nize repairs or sub­sti­tu­tions, compare two pieces of appar­ently similar quality, and judge whether an object matches its claimed mater­ial or origin.famil­iar goods and obvious defects may be judged untrained. train­ing becomes import­ant when value depends on rare mater­i­als, subtle work­man­ship, con­cealed repairs, spe­cial­ist con­struc­tion, or a con­vin­cing imit­a­tion.appraisal exam­ines the object itself. com­merce con­cerns the market, pro­spect­ive buyers, and terms of sale. a rel­ev­ant craft may reveal tech­nical flaws that a general appraisal cannot estab­lish.athleticsusual attribute: strength untrained: yesath­let­ics covers force­ful or sus­tained phys­ical move­ment. its ordin­ary uses include climb­ing a rough wall or rope, pulling oneself over a ledge, swim­ming through dif­fi­cult water, sprint­ing across demand­ing ground, clear­ing a ditch, or jumping high enough to seize a hand­hold.79skills · acrobatics – athletics

pages.title: Bluff · Cartography
pages.text: skillsathletics – diplomacyathletics · continuedthe sur­round­ing con­di­tions determ­ine what makes the attempt uncer­tain: poor holds, heavy water, unstable ground, awkward equip­ment, exhaus­tion, or similar com­plic­a­tions. move­ment demand­ing balance or precise body control may use acro­bat­ics instead.bluffusual attribute: charisma untrained: yesbluff lets a char­ac­ter present false­hood, mis­dir­ec­tion, or con­cealed intent as some­thing plaus­ible. it covers spoken lies, feigned con­fid­ence, mis­lead­ing beha­vior, inven­ted explan­a­tions, and dis­trac­tions created through words or conduct.a decep­tion becomes easier to believe when it fits what the listener already expects and agrees with the evid­ence at hand. firsthand know­ledge, obvious con­tra­dic­tions, close scru­tiny, or a story that demands too much faith make the attempt harder.at a city gate, a trav­eler might claim that a delayed wagon is expec­ted inside, answer ques­tions with rehearsed con­fid­ence, and keep the guard's atten­tion away from a com­pan­ion. pre­par­ing a false pass would call for forgery, while taking the guard's key would call for sleight of hand.cartographyusual attribute: intelligence untrained: limitedcar­to­graphy covers reading, copying, cor­rect­ing, and cre­at­ing maps. a car­to­grapher can inter­pret symbols and scale, compare con­flict­ing maps, trans­late meas­ure­ments and route notes into a usable rep­res­ent­a­tion, update a map after the land­scape has changed, and recog­nize when dis­tances, land­marks, or terrain do not fit together.anyone may sketch a famil­iar road or mark a remembered land­mark. pro­du­cing an accur­ate working map, repair­ing an incom­plete chart, or com­bin­ing several imper­fect accounts requires train­ing.car­to­graphy records what is known about the land. nav­ig­a­tion uses that inform­a­tion, together with obser­va­tion and remembered geo­graphy, to determ­ine pos­i­tion and course.commandusual attribute: charisma untrained: yescommand gives clear orders, assigns imme­di­ate respons­ib­il­it­ies, and keeps people working together when speed, danger, noise, or con­fu­sion could break their coordin­a­tion. it applies to a crew, patrol, work gang, nearby mil­it­ary unit, or similar group the char­ac­ter can per­son­ally direct.a com­mander might assign a patrol to several entrances, organ­ize workers around a col­lapsing struc­ture, call a deck crew to prepare for a squall, or restore order after con­flict­ing instruc­tions. the skill helps make pri­or­it­ies under­stood and keeps atten­tion on the shared task.command is per­sonal and imme­di­ate: the char­ac­ter must be able to com­mu­nic­ate with the group and observe the work closely enough to direct it. use mass combat when dir­ect­ing form­a­tions in battle and the ruler system when gov­ern­ing estates, armies, courts, fac­tions, or coun­tries.commerceusual attribute: intelligence untrained: yescom­merce is prac­tical know­ledge of markets, trade customs, con­tracts, supply, bar­gain­ing, and the move­ment of goods. it helps a char­ac­ter locate buyers or sellers, recog­nize scarcity or unusual prices, under­stand the terms of a trans­ac­tion, and judge how mer­chand­ise reaches a region.a mer­chant might identify the market most likely to accept foreign coin, dis­cover which caravan con­trols the local salt supply, nego­ti­ate a bulk pur­chase, or notice that a con­tract quietly trans­fers an unusual risk to the buyer. avail­able altern­at­ives, urgency, repu­ta­tion, and know­ledge of the market all shape the bargain.appraisal can estab­lish the work­man­ship and likely value of a jeweled cup. com­merce finds the buyer who wants it, pre­dicts what that buyer may pay, and nego­ti­ates the terms of sale.craft (field)usual attribute: varies untrained: limitedcraft governs the prac­tical work of a learned trade, from select­ing mater­i­als and plan­ning the task through shaping, fitting, assem­bling, fin­ish­ing, and repair. each field is a sep­ar­ate skill.80skills · athletics – craft (field)

pages.title: Skill Mastery: Craft (Specific Field) · Cryptography
pages.text: skillsathletics – diplomacycraft (field) · continueda trained craft­sper­son can follow or adapt a sound design, dia­gnose why an object failed, judge what a repair requires, fit an item to its inten­ded user or purpose, and estim­ate the tools, mater­i­als, and labor needed for the work.the gov­ern­ing attrib­ute follows the task. heavy forging may use strength, fine assembly may use dex­ter­ity, and design, dia­gnosis, or tech­nical eval­u­ation may use intel­li­gence. the quality of the mater­i­als, tools, facil­it­ies, plans, and time avail­able shapes what work can reas­on­ably be attemp­ted.metal and stone: armor­smith­ing; black­smith­ing; gold­smith­ing; jewelry; lock­smith­ing; masonry; smelt­ing; weapon­smith­ing.wood and trans­port: boat­build­ing and ship­wright­ing; bow­mak­ing and fletch­ing; car­pentry; cartwright­ing; instru­ment making; wheel­wright­ing; wood­carving.cloth and leather: cob­bling; cos­tum­ing; dyeing; embroid­ery; leather­work­ing; tail­or­ing and sewing; tanning; weaving.fine and house­hold work: book­bind­ing; cal­li­graphy and illu­min­a­tion; gem­cut­ting; glass­work­ing; paint­ing; pottery; rope­mak­ing; sculp­ture; trap­mak­ing.food and com­pounds: alchemy (mundane); brewing; cooking; wine­mak­ing.frames: golem frames.craft (golem frames) governs the fitting, main­ten­ance, con­struc­tion, and repair of eli­gible ordin­ary golem frame struc­ture and mech­an­isms. the ded­ic­ated golem frames repair rules state what damage each method can restore and what addi­tional train­ing, mater­ial, magic, access, or work­shop facil­it­ies it requires.black­smith­ing covers ordin­ary forged tools; armor­smith­ing and weapon­smith­ing handle their spe­cial­ist work. alchemy (mundane) pro­duces non­ma­gical com­pounds. a rel­ev­ant craft can expose tech­nical flaws and repair needs, while appraisal judges broader quality and likely value.mas­ter­work and rare-mater­ial equip­ment use the mater­ial and special-con­struc­tion rules in equip­ment. magical con­struc­tion, magical potions, and excep­tional craft (field) · continuedammuni­tion require addi­tional train­ing or abil­it­ies. whenever such work is per­mit­ted, the rel­ev­ant craft governs its exe­cu­tion.skill mastery: craft (specific field)craft skill mastery belongs to one spe­cific craft field. a char­ac­ter who learns skill mastery for craft (weapon­smith­ing), for example, does not gain it for craft (armor­smith­ing), craft (black­smith­ing), or any other field.a char­ac­ter with the applic­able craft skill mastery may attempt to make steel or tanso-steel equip­ment at mas­ter­work quality. appro­pri­ate mater­i­als, tools, facil­it­ies, and time are required.working mithril or adam­antite requires the rel­ev­ant craft skill mastery in addi­tion to every mater­ial-spe­cific require­ment; mastery alone grants no access to either mater­ial. magical con­struc­tion, pre­par­a­tion for enchant­ment, and unusual items retain their sep­ar­ate require­ments.cryptographyusual attribute: intelligence untrained: trained onlycryp­to­graphy covers recog­niz­ing, cre­at­ing, and deci­pher­ing delib­er­ate codes and ciphers. it exam­ines repeated symbols, sub­sti­tu­tions, pat­terns, keys, con­ven­tional open­ings, and the struc­ture of a message to under­stand how its con­tents have been con­cealed.a cryp­to­grapher might compare several inter­cep­ted mes­sages for a shared system, prepare a message using an estab­lished code, recog­nize that appar­ently ordin­ary writing con­tains an encoded pattern, or work from context and sur­viv­ing frag­ments to recon­struct a cipher.deci­pher­ing the code reveals the message as written; it does not grant fluency in its lan­guage. unfa­mil­iar lan­guages and scripts use lin­guist­ics or the rel­ev­ant know­ledge field.diplomacyusual attribute: charisma untrained: yesdip­lomacy per­suades, nego­ti­ates, medi­ates dis­putes, and presents terms in a form another person may accept. it can secure a hearing, request aid or access, improve strained rela­tions, broker an exchange, calm a dispute, or find a work­able com­prom­ise between com­pet­ing interests.81skills · craft (field) – diplomacy

pages.title: Engineering · Skill Mastery: Engineering
pages.text: skillsdiplomacy – forgerydiplomacy · continueda char­ac­ter might per­suade a sus­pi­cious offi­cial to review new evid­ence, nego­ti­ate safe passage through con­tested ter­rit­ory, help two guilds agree on shared access to a ware­house, or con­vince rivals to cooper­ate against an imme­di­ate danger. the pro­posal may offer con­ces­sions, appeal to shared values, protect every­one's dignity, or show how agree­ment serves each party.people weigh a pro­posal against their author­ity, oblig­a­tions, interests, trust, and avail­able altern­at­ives. a friendly offi­cial may grant a modest favor after a cour­teous request. a truce between com­mit­ted enemies needs com­pel­ling lever­age and terms both sides can survive accept­ing.in a formal court, etiquette helps the peti­tioner choose the proper title, timing, and manner of approach. dip­lomacy shapes the request itself and gives the listener a reason to con­sider it.engineeringusual attribute: intelligence untrained: trained onlyengin­eer­ing covers the design and ana­lysis of struc­tures, machines, for­ti­fic­a­tions, bridges, water­works, and com­par­able con­struc­ted systems. it con­siders sup­ports, loads, stresses, moving parts, mater­i­als, drain­age, and likely points of failure.a sagging bridge can be examined for failing sup­ports, a hoist judged against its inten­ded load, and a for­ti­fic­a­tion studied for vul­ner­able points. engin­eer­ing also plans the passage of water through a mill or set­tle­ment and tests whether a pro­posed alter­a­tion will weaken a larger struc­ture.engin­eer­ing sup­plies the design and tech­nical judg­ment. the rel­ev­ant craft carries out con­struc­tion, fitting, and repair.engineering · continuedfor golem frames, engin­eer­ing sup­plies dia­gnosis, plans, load ana­lysis, and tech­nical design; craft (golem frames) carries out eli­gible phys­ical work. golem frames owns the repair limits and required facil­it­ies.skill mastery: engineeringengin­eer­ing skill mastery allows a char­ac­ter to devise an ori­ginal struc­ture, machine, for­ti­fic­a­tion, or integ­rated system when no estab­lished plan or close pre­ced­ent is avail­able. a suc­cess­ful design accounts for the inten­ded purpose, avail­able mater­i­als, oper­at­ing con­di­tions, and likely points of failure.appro­pri­ate time, inform­a­tion, draft­ing tools, and access to the site, plans, mech­an­ism, or com­par­able evid­ence are still required.engin­eer­ing pro­duces the design and tech­nical instruc­tions. the rel­ev­ant craft governs con­struc­tion, fitting, and repair. pro­jects under­taken by an estate, army, set­tle­ment, or faction use the ruler system for labor, resources, and com­ple­tion; combat or mass combat governs any bat­tle­field effect of the fin­ished work.escape artistusual attribute: dexterity untrained: yesescape artist uses flex­ib­il­ity, lever­age, and careful move­ment to slip bonds, work free of a net or entangling wrap, squeeze through a con­fined opening, or release a trapped limb. a char­ac­ter might search for slack in tied wrists, turn the body through a gap barely large enough to permit passage, or free a boot caught between stones.the restraint must leave some plaus­ible room, weak­ness, or lever­age to exploit. opening a locked restraint calls for locks and traps.grapples always use the combat pro­ced­ure; escape artist never sub­sti­tutes for or assists that check.82skills · diplomacy – escape artist

pages.title: Etiquette · Skill Mastery: Etiquette
pages.text: skillsdiplomacy – forgeryetiquetteusual attribute: charisma untrained: yesetiquette is fluency in the manners, titles, cere­mon­ies, and expect­a­tions of struc­tured society. it helps a char­ac­ter choose the proper form of address, make intro­duc­tions, exchange gifts, observe pre­ced­ence, dress for an occa­sion, and move through formal gath­er­ings without cre­at­ing an unin­ten­ded insult.the skill can also reveal meaning carried through cere­mony. a change in seating may signal favor or dis­grace; an omitted title may be a care­less mistake or a delib­er­ate slight; an unusu­ally valu­able gift may create an expect­a­tion that nobody states aloud.famil­iar customs are usually straight­for­ward. foreign courts, obscure rites, old mil­it­ary tra­di­tions, and cere­mon­ies designed to test an out­sider may be con­sid­er­ably harder to nav­ig­ate.skill mastery: etiquetteetiquette skill mastery allows a char­ac­ter to design a complex cere­mony, formal recep­tion, or order of pre­ced­ence that brings several known tra­di­tions together without cre­at­ing unin­ten­ded insults or con­tra­dic­tions.the char­ac­ter must first under­stand the customs being incor­por­ated. a rel­ev­ant know­ledge skill may be needed for an unfa­mil­iar faith, court, mil­it­ary tra­di­tion, or culture.etiquette determ­ines the correct forms, honors, and cere­mo­nial arrange­ment. dip­lomacy remains respons­ible for nego­ti­at­ing accept­ance, resolv­ing oppos­i­tion, and per­suad­ing par­ti­cipants to cooper­ate.forgeryusual attribute: dexterity untrained: limitedforgery is used to create or alter doc­u­ments, imitate hand­writ­ing, repro­duce seals, and falsify records. it can change a name, date, amount, or author­iz­a­tion; create a pass or letter from a suit­able example; insert a plaus­ible entry into a ledger; or repro­duce the visible marks by which an insti­tu­tion recog­nizes its doc­u­ments.the same train­ing helps examine sus­pi­cious writing. a prac­ticed forger may recog­nize incon­sist­ent strokes, an incor­rectly repro­duced seal, an alter­a­tion con­cealed beneath later work, or methods famil­iar from other false doc­u­ments.basic alter­a­tions may be attemp­ted untrained. con­vin­cing offi­cial records, unfa­mil­iar scripts, closely con­trolled seals, and other tech­nical work require train­ing, suit­able examples, and appro­pri­ate mater­i­als. phys­ical coun­ter­feits such as coins use the rel­ev­ant craft.skill mastery: forgeryforgery skill mastery allows a char­ac­ter to create a con­nec­ted body of false records whose dates, ref­er­ences, author­it­ies, sig­na­tures, seals, and entries support one another. this can estab­lish a con­vin­cing paper trail across several doc­u­ments rather than relying on a single isol­ated false­hood.the attempt requires suit­able mater­i­als and enough genuine examples to repro­duce the insti­tu­tion's forms and identi­fy­ing marks.research may be needed to dis­cover the records, pro­ced­ures, names, and past events with which the false doc­u­ments must agree. forgery creates and alters the doc­u­ments them­selves; phys­ical coun­ter­feits such as coins remain the work of the rel­ev­ant craft.83skills · etiquette – forgery

pages.title: Gaming · Golem Piloting
pages.text: skillsgaming – knowledge (field)gamingusual attribute: intelligence untrained: yesgaming covers the rules, cus­tom­ary play, strategy, odds, and table con­ven­tions of games of chance or skill. it helps a char­ac­ter judge a pos­i­tion, choose sound play, recog­nize an exper­i­enced oppon­ent, assess risk, and learn an unfa­mil­iar game through obser­va­tion and explan­a­tion.during play, gaming may reveal that an oppon­ent is setting up a famil­iar strategy, that a wager is poor for the appar­ent odds, or that a local rule changes the value of an oth­er­wise strong move. it also helps dis­tin­guish ordin­ary custom from beha­vior that should draw sus­pi­cion.a cheater may use bluff to mislead oppon­ents or sleight of hand to manip­u­late cards, dice, or pieces. gaming sup­plies the under­stand­ing needed to choose a useful decep­tion and recog­nize the risks involved.golem pilotingusual attribute: dexterity  untrained: limitedgolem pilot­ing governs oper­a­tion of an elven-inter­face golem frame: delib­er­ate loco­motion, dif­fi­cult terrain, close man­euv­er­ing, jumps, falls, forced move­ment, unstable footing, damaged con­trols, melee hand­ling, and active defens­ive hand­ling.routine walking, turning, and com­par­able oper­a­tion need no check for a qual­i­fied pilot. when an uncer­tain con­sequen­tial task requires a check, use the com­plete ordin­ary skill pro­ced­ure. untrained use is limited to the expli­cit emer­gency-oper­a­tion pro­ced­ure; it does not make the oper­ator a qual­i­fied pilot.frame combat also derives a small flat pilot­ing com­pet­ence mod­i­fier from the gov­ern­ing golem pilot­ing attrib­ute. that mod­i­fier is not the pilot's skill threshold and is used only where the golem frames rules expressly call for it.golem sensesusual attribute: wisdom  untrained: yes — requires training in golem pilotinggolem senses governs inter­pret­a­tion of a frame's sensory feed: peri­pheral threats, rapidly chan­ging pos­i­tions, com­mu­nic­a­tions, damaged sensors, poor vis­ib­il­ity, and inform­a­tion over­load.a char­ac­ter trained in golem pilot­ing may attempt golem senses untrained. begin with half wisdom, rounded down, then apply the normal dif­fi­culty, frame golem senses · continuedsensor and situ­ation mod­i­fi­ers. this does not grant golem senses or waive any frame-oper­a­tion require­ment. char­ac­ters without golem pilot­ing cannot use this untrained excep­tion. golem ranged train­ing remains sep­ar­ately required for ranged weapons.simple obvious threats need no check. when broader bat­tle­field aware­ness matters, use the one-check-per-round pro­ced­ure and mod­i­fi­ers in golem frames. golem senses determ­ines whether applic­able threats permit aware defense; it is not an attack skill and does not replace ordin­ary per­cep­tion outside frame oper­a­tion.investigationusual attribute: intelligence untrained: yesinvest­ig­a­tion covers delib­er­ate exam­in­a­tion of a place, object, account, or chain of events. it searches for rel­ev­ant traces, com­pares state­ments with phys­ical evid­ence, tests pos­sible explan­a­tions, recog­nizes con­nec­tions, and recon­structs what most likely happened.a char­ac­ter might determ­ine how someone entered a locked room, estab­lish which damage occurred first, notice that a scene was rearranged, compare several wit­nesses' accounts, or connect an appar­ently ordin­ary object to an earlier event. incom­plete, damaged, or delib­er­ately mis­lead­ing evid­ence may support only a partial con­clu­sion.per­cep­tion might reveal fresh mud beneath a window. invest­ig­a­tion con­nects it to the forced latch and the foot­prints outside. research can then follow a maker's mark or own­er­ship record through an archive.intimidationusual attribute: charisma untrained: yesintim­id­a­tion pres­sures another person toward hes­it­a­tion, com­pli­ance, retreat, silence, or dis­clos­ure through menace, author­ity, fear, or a cred­ible threat. it can make a bel­li­ger­ent stranger recon­sider a fight, compel a tres­passer to leave, silence delib­er­ate dis­rup­tion, or press a frightened captive for an answer.the target's courage, oblig­a­tions, avail­able altern­at­ives, and belief in the threat shape both the dif­fi­culty and the response. intim­id­a­tion remains con­vin­cing while the danger and the char­ac­ter's ability to carry it out remain cred­ible.84skills · gaming – intimidation

pages.title: Knowledge (Field) · Rumors of Thaumaturgy
pages.text: skillsgaming – knowledge (field)intimidation · continuedcha­risma is usual when the char­ac­ter relies on pres­ence, tone, or author­ity. phys­ical dom­in­ance may use strength. a precise threat based on com­prom­ising records, legal expos­ure, or care­fully assembled know­ledge may use intel­li­gence.knowledge (field)usual attribute: intelligence untrained: trained onlyknow­ledge covers learned inform­a­tion within a par­tic­u­lar field. each field is a sep­ar­ate skill. a check may recall a fact, recog­nize a person, place, object, prac­tice, or phe­nomenon con­nec­ted to the subject, inter­pret evid­ence through that dis­cip­line, explain its sig­ni­fic­ance, or connect several pieces of learned inform­a­tion.common inform­a­tion that requires no spe­cial­ist edu­ca­tion may use an ordin­ary intel­li­gence check. a trained-only know­ledge check applies when the ques­tion depends on study within the named field.the obscur­ity, age, loc­al­ity, and spe­cial­ist nature of the inform­a­tion shape the dif­fi­culty. know­ledge (her­aldry) might identify a house from a damaged badge, know­ledge (geology) might explain an unusual seam in a cavern wall, and know­ledge (reli­gion) might place an unfa­mil­iar rite within a known faith.use the single best-fitting know­ledge skill for one ques­tion. broad and narrow fields do not stack and do not provide several attempts at the same fact. spe­cificity changes dif­fi­culty: an obscure tasla­maran geo­graph­ical fact may be extreme for know­ledge (geo­graphy) and easy or normal for know­ledge (tasla­maran geo­graphy).natural world and places: anatomy; botany; creatures (a spe­cific family); geo­graphy; geology; local know­ledge (a spe­cific place); nature.history and society: ancient history; archae­ology and ruins; her­aldry; history; law; nobil­ity and gene­a­logy; polit­ics; tactics; under­world.thought, belief, and lan­guage: astro­logy; folk­lore; know­ledge (lan­guage: spe­cific lan­guage); occult; philo­sophy; reli­gion; spirits; theo­logy.tech­nical and magical study: astro­nomy; magic; math­em­at­ics; metal­lurgy; planes and cos­mo­logy; spell­craft.know­ledge (magic) covers broad magical schol­ar­ship: magical tra­di­tions, com­monly recog­nized spells, magical creatures, objects, phe­nom­ena, and general theory.know­ledge (spell­craft) studies how spells are con­struc­ted and operate. it can identify a spell as it is cast, decipher another caster's research, and analyze active knowledge (field) · continuedor recor­ded magical effects. it is trained only. char­ac­ters outside mage jobs may learn spell­craft. the field sup­plies tech­nical know­ledge; per­mis­sion to cast, create, or research spells comes from the rel­ev­ant magical train­ing. the current iden­ti­fic­a­tion and deci­pher­ing pro­ced­ures appear under spells and spellcast­ing — know­ledge (spell­craft).know­ledge (tactics) covers learned mil­it­ary prin­ciples and ana­lysis. combat, mass combat, and the ruler system determ­ine how that know­ledge is applied at char­ac­ter, bat­tle­field, and ruler scale.a learned know­ledge (lan­guage: spe­cific lan­guage) field grants ordin­ary fluency in that lan­guage without requir­ing checks for routine con­ver­sa­tion or reading. archaic forms, unusual dia­lects, tech­nical usage, damaged writing, and com­par­able uncer­tainty may call for a check. lin­guist­ics covers com­par­at­ive lan­guage study and recon­struc­tion across lan­guages.rumors of thaumaturgyfrag­ment­ary writ­ings some­times speak of thau­mat­urgy, a hidden dis­cip­line said to reach beyond con­ven­tional magical schol­ar­ship. no recog­nized school openly teaches it, and reli­able accounts are exceed­ingly rare.85skills · intimidation – knowledge (field)

pages.title: Linguistics · Skill Mastery: Linguistics
pages.text: skillslinguistics – performance (field)linguisticsusual attribute: intelligence untrained: trained onlylin­guist­ics is the com­par­at­ive study of lan­guage, scripts, dia­lects, trans­la­tion, ety­mo­logy, and accents. it can identify the family or region from which a lan­guage developed, dis­tin­guish closely related dia­lects, recog­nize bor­rowed words, compare dif­fer­ent ver­sions of a text, and explain what an accent or unusual con­struc­tion sug­gests about a speaker or writer.the skill also helps trans­late unfa­mil­iar or archaic pas­sages when related lan­guages and suf­fi­cient context provide a basis for com­par­ison. a lin­guist may recon­struct missing words from grammar, recover part of a damaged inscrip­tion, or determ­ine how a term's meaning changed between periods, although the sur­viv­ing evid­ence may limit the cer­tainty or com­plete­ness of the reading.fluency in a par­tic­u­lar lan­guage comes from its spe­cific know­ledge field. delib­er­ate codes and ciphers use cryp­to­graphy.skill mastery: linguisticsgiven a sub­stan­tial body of related sur­viv­ing texts and enough time to compare them, a char­ac­ter with lin­guist­ics skill mastery may attempt to recon­struct a pro­vi­sional grammar and lexicon for an unknown or dead lan­guage. the recon­struc­tion provides a basis for later lin­guist­ics checks to trans­late pas­sages sup­por­ted by that evid­ence.its con­clu­sions are limited by the sur­viv­ing texts and cannot supply missing vocab­u­lary, grammar, or meaning for which no evid­ence exists.this recon­struc­tion grants neither con­ver­sa­tional nor routine reading fluency; fluency still requires the appro­pri­ate know­ledge (lan­guage: spe­cific lan­guage) skill. delib­er­ate codes and ciphers remain the province of cryp­to­graphy.locks and trapsusual attribute: dexterity untrained: limitedlocks and traps covers examin­ing, opening, bypassing, dis­arm­ing, and reset­ting mech­an­ical locks and traps. it allows a char­ac­ter to under­stand how a mech­an­ism is arranged, identify the part that holds or releases it, and manip­u­late its com­pon­ents without relying on force alone.locks and traps · continueda char­ac­ter might work a lock, release a trapped catch, isolate a trigger, hold a mech­an­ism safe while someone passes, or restore a dis­armed device to working order. a simple exposed mech­an­ism may permit an untrained attempt; skilled locks, con­cealed mech­an­isms, and haz­ard­ous traps require train­ing.per­cep­tion may catch a faint seam, dis­placed dust, or unusual tension; invest­ig­a­tion may uncover the device through a delib­er­ate search. locks and traps handles the mech­an­ism once found. craft (lock­smith­ing) and craft (trap­mak­ing) create and repair such devices.skill mastery: locks and trapslocks and traps skill mastery allows a char­ac­ter to open, bypass, disable, or reset a mech­an­ical device while pre­serving it and con­ceal­ing signs of inter­fer­ence. a later exam­iner may still dis­cover the work through invest­ig­a­tion or locks and traps.the attempt still requires access to the mech­an­ism, suit­able tools, and whatever time the work nat­ur­ally demands.per­cep­tion may reveal an imme­di­ate sign of danger, and invest­ig­a­tion may locate a con­cealed device or recon­struct what happened. locks and traps manip­u­lates the mech­an­ism; the rel­ev­ant craft creates or repairs it. a wholly magical ward must be addressed through magic. when a ward has a mech­an­ical trigger, this mastery can affect that mech­an­ism without sup­press­ing the ward itself.medicineusual attribute: wisdom untrained: limitedmedi­cine governs dia­gnosis, pro­gnosis, con­tinu­ing care, pre­ven­tion, and ordin­ary treat­ment. a trained char­ac­ter can examine symp­toms and injur­ies, judge their sever­ity and likely pro­gres­sion, choose appro­pri­ate mundane care, and monitor whether a patient is recov­er­ing as expec­ted.its ordin­ary prac­tice includes clean­ing and dress­ing injur­ies, recog­niz­ing signs of disease or poison, setting rest and san­it­a­tion require­ments, select­ing a suit­able diet or medi­cine, determ­in­ing a safe dose, and adjust­ing care when a patient's con­di­tion changes.an untrained char­ac­ter may recog­nize obvious dis­tress, provide simple care, or follow instruc­tions from a trained care­giver. tech­nical dia­gnosis, com­plic­ated treat­ment, and pro­fes­sional con­tinu­ing care require train­ing.86skills · linguistics – medicine

pages.title: Skill Mastery: Medicine · Navigation
pages.text: skillslinguistics – performance (field)medicine · continuedmedi­cine determ­ines how a known medi­cine or ingredi­ent should be used. finding and identi­fy­ing suit­able plants in the field may also require know­ledge (botany), sur­vival, or another rel­ev­ant skill.related feat: field medic. field medic handles urgent care under pres­sure; medi­cine sup­ports dia­gnosis and con­tinu­ing care before and after the crisis.skill mastery: medicinemedi­cine skill mastery unlocks advanced medical prac­tice. a char­ac­ter with this mastery can dia­gnose obscure dis­eases, poisons, and com­plic­ated injur­ies, then plan advanced con­tinu­ing care. the char­ac­ter can also choose a mundane course of treat­ment and prepare the required medi­cine when ingredi­ents, tools, and time are avail­able.use the ordin­ary medi­cine check when the outcome remains uncer­tain; the mastery adds per­mis­sions, not a flat bonus. field medic still governs urgent bleed­ing and mortal-wound treat­ment.finding ingredi­ents may call for know­ledge (botany), sur­vival, or another applic­able skill. all treat­ment provided by this mastery is mundane and cannot regrow missing tissue.navigationusual attribute: intelligence untrained: limitednav­ig­a­tion determ­ines pos­i­tion, chooses a route, and keeps a journey on course by using land­marks, maps, stars, instru­ments, or remembered geo­graphy. on land, it may compare visible terrain with a map, choose between known roads or cross­ings, retrace a route, or main­tain dir­ec­tion where no road exists. at sea, it may estab­lish pos­i­tion, account for drift, and plot a course from obser­va­tions.an untrained char­ac­ter may follow obvious land­marks or a clearly marked route. uncer­tain pos­i­tion, poor vis­ib­il­ity, open water, and other tech­nical or haz­ard­ous nav­ig­a­tion require train­ing.aboard a vessel, the nav­ig­ator plots and main­tains the course from maps and obser­va­tions; the crew uses seaman­ship to carry out the needed changes in sail and helm.navigation · continuedskill mastery: navigationnav­ig­a­tion skill mastery unlocks dead reck­on­ing. a char­ac­ter with this mastery can estim­ate the current pos­i­tion and recover a course from a reli­able last known pos­i­tion, using whatever frag­ment­ary obser­va­tions remain, such as elapsed travel, dir­ec­tion, speed, terrain, winds, cur­rents, or partial sight­ings.dead reck­on­ing requires usable inform­a­tion and cannot supply a missing obser­va­tion or start­ing pos­i­tion. incom­plete inform­a­tion may limit the pre­ci­sion of the result.dead reck­on­ing does not keep a char­ac­ter from becom­ing lost, reveal another creature's trail, or grant the track­ing or pathfind­ing talents.perceptionusual attribute: wisdom untrained: yesper­cep­tion is used when the imme­di­ate ques­tion is what the char­ac­ter's senses reveal. it covers move­ment, sound, scent, changes in the sur­round­ings, con­cealed objects, and creatures attempt­ing to remain unnoticed.a char­ac­ter might hear quiet move­ment beyond a door, smell smoke before seeing a flame, catch a distant figure break­ing the skyline, notice a sudden draft, spot an object partly con­cealed beneath fur­niture, or pick out a creature hiding among natural cover. per­cep­tion may operate when some­thing draws atten­tion or when the char­ac­ter delib­er­ately watches, listens, or exam­ines the imme­di­ate scene.light­ing, dis­tance, noise, dis­trac­tion, and con­ceal­ment shape how dif­fi­cult a detail is to notice. con­nect­ing several details or recon­struct­ing the event that pro­duced them uses invest­ig­a­tion.performance (field)usual attribute: charisma untrained: yesper­form­ance uses a prac­ticed art to enter­tain, impress, move, dis­tract, or com­mu­nic­ate with an audi­ence. each field is a sep­ar­ate skill. a per­former can choose suit­able mater­ial, prepare or rehearse it, adapt the deliv­ery to the setting, sustain an audi­ence's atten­tion, and convey a mood, story, argu­ment, or char­ac­ter through the chosen art.87skills · medicine – performance (field)

pages.title: Profession (Field) · Research
pages.text: skillsperformance (field) – sense motiveperformance (field) · continuedthe audi­ence, venue, noise, pre­par­a­tion, famili­ar­ity of the mater­ial, and expect­a­tions sur­round­ing the occa­sion shape the dif­fi­culty. a tavern song for an eager crowd asks for some­thing dif­fer­ent from a formal recital before a foreign court or an impro­vised speech meant to hold a frightened gath­er­ing together.cha­risma is usual when recep­tion and pres­ence matter most. a dif­fer­ent attrib­ute may govern a per­form­ance when its method depends more strongly on phys­ical pre­ci­sion, memory, endur­ance, or another quality.common fields include acting; dance; instru­ment (a spe­cific family); jug­gling; oratory; poetry and recit­a­tion; singing; storytelling; and vent­ri­lo­quism.profession (field)usual attribute: varies untrained: trained onlypro­fes­sion rep­res­ents the broad prac­tical know­ledge and judg­ment of a live­li­hood. each field is learned sep­ar­ately. it covers the occu­pa­tion's routine work, working con­di­tions, cus­tom­ary stand­ards, hazards, records, tools, mater­i­als, and rela­tion­ships with employ­ers, cus­tom­ers, sup­pli­ers, or fellow prac­ti­tion­ers.a pro­fes­sional can plan an ordin­ary workday, estim­ate common needs and delays, recog­nize when con­di­tions are unsafe or unusual, super­vise routine labor, main­tain the records expec­ted of the trade, and under­stand how people in that occu­pa­tion usually solve famil­iar prob­lems. the exact attrib­ute follows the task and the pro­fes­sion.narrow spe­cial­ist work uses its ded­ic­ated skill. a pro­fes­sion (sailor) under­stands watches, duties, cargo routines, and life aboard ship, while seaman­ship con­trols the vessel. pro­fes­sion (steward or sen­eschal) covers the ordin­ary work of a house­hold or estate; the ruler system governs the insti­tu­tion itself.pro­fes­sion (soldier) covers mil­it­ary routine, service customs, camp duties, and the ordin­ary work of sol­dier­ing. weapon use and combat man­euvers follow the char­ac­ter's actual train­ing and the combat rules.land and resources: agri­cul­ture; fisher; for­ester; gardener; hunter; miner; shep­herd; trapper or furrier; wood­cut­ter.trade and trans­port: baker; butcher; driver or team­ster; mer­chant; miller; porter; sailor.ser­vices and insti­tu­tions: bar­ris­ter; clerk; groom or stable­keeper; innkeeper; lib­rar­ian; midwife; scribe; soldier; steward or sen­eschal.researchusual attribute: intelligence untrained: limitedresearch finds, com­pares, and assesses inform­a­tion held in books, ledgers, archives, cata­logues, cor­res­pond­ence, maps, and similar organ­ized sources. it follows ref­er­ences, recon­ciles con­flict­ing accounts, recog­nizes gaps in a record, and draws a sup­por­ted answer from mater­ial scattered across several sources.guild ledgers can trace own­er­ship; maps and travel accounts may pre­serve an older name for a ruin; con­flict­ing chron­icles can be com­pared for what they agree upon. cor­res­pond­ence may pre­serve a for­got­ten agree­ment, while a library cata­logue can identify where a needed text is held.a clear answer in a famil­iar source may be found untrained. obscure, extens­ive, con­tra­dict­ory, or poorly organ­ized mater­ial requires train­ing. research estab­lishes what the sur­viv­ing sources contain; rel­ev­ant know­ledge helps the char­ac­ter under­stand spe­cial­ist subject matter found within them.rideusual attribute: dexterity untrained: yesride covers mount­ing, guiding, stop­ping, turning, and keeping one's seat on a riding animal. routine travel on a calm, trained mount usually needs no check.a check may become appro­pri­ate when the mount stumbles or rears, the rider must nego­ti­ate steep or crowded ground, a sudden turn or obstacle threatens the rider's seat, or the animal must be guided through imme­di­ate 88skills · performance (field) – ride

pages.title: Ropework · Seamanship
pages.text: skillsperformance (field) – sense motiveride · continueddanger. the skill reflects what the rider does from the saddle rather than chan­ging what the animal has been taught.when the dif­fi­culty comes from the animal's present beha­vior, use animal hand­ling. when it comes from what the animal has been taught, use animal train­ing.ropeworkusual attribute: dexterity untrained: yesrope­work covers choos­ing and tying knots, making lash­ings and hitches, joining lines, secur­ing loads, and judging whether a fasten­ing will hold. it may be used to anchor a climb­ing line, lash cargo to a wagon, fasten a boat, secure a shelter, join two ropes, make an impro­vised loop or harness, or release a knot tightened by strain and weather.the rope, anchor, load, access, and con­di­tions determ­ine how demand­ing the work is. rope­work can assess the fasten­ing being made, but damaged rope or an unsound anchor remains a phys­ical weak­ness.making rope is craft (rope­mak­ing). once it is in hand, rope­work governs its knots and fasten­ings; aboard ship, seaman­ship governs the wider oper­a­tion they support.seamanshipusual attribute: dexterity untrained: limitedseaman­ship covers the demand­ing oper­a­tion of boats and ships. it includes hand­ling sails and rigging, steer­ing, coordin­at­ing prac­tical crew work, and keeping a vessel under control as wind, current, water, or damage changes its beha­vior.its ordin­ary uses include setting or redu­cing sail, bring­ing a vessel along­side a pier, steer­ing through dif­fi­cult water, respond­ing to a sudden change in wind, and com­pens­at­ing for damaged rigging or other prob­lems that affect control. basic work under dir­ec­tion may be attemp­ted untrained; oper­at­ing a vessel inde­pend­ently or under haz­ard­ous con­di­tions requires train­ing.nav­ig­a­tion estab­lishes where the vessel should go. seaman­ship handles the vessel that must get there. within the broader pro­fes­sion (sailor), seaman­ship is the spe­cial­ist skill for con­trolling the vessel itself.sense motiveusual attribute: wisdom untrained: yessense motive reads emo­tional state, sin­cer­ity, guarded interests, and likely inten­tion through beha­vior and context. it can reveal unease, eager­ness, con­cealed hos­til­ity, divided loyalty, a rehearsed answer, or signs that someone is trying to steer the con­ver­sa­tion.a mer­chant may appear reluct­ant while showing every sign of wanting the sale com­pleted quickly. an envoy may speak warmly while repeatedly check­ing the exits. a pris­oner may react more strongly to one name than to 89skills · ride – sense motive

pages.title: Sleight of Hand · Stealth
pages.text: skillssense motive – additional skills and fieldssense motive · continuedthe accus­a­tion being dis­cussed. sense motive weighs these details together with tone, timing, and cir­cum­stance.the result is an impres­sion groun­ded in what the char­ac­ter can observe. strong evid­ence may support a clear con­clu­sion; mixed or subtle beha­vior may support only sus­pi­cion, uncer­tainty, or several plaus­ible read­ings.sleight of handusual attribute: dexterity untrained: yessleight of hand uses quick, con­trolled move­ment to palm, conceal, pass, switch, or remove a small object without attract­ing notice. it can slip a coin into a sleeve, exchange one small object for another, pass some­thing between com­pan­ions, hide an item during a search, manip­u­late a game piece, or take advant­age of a brief dis­trac­tion.the object's size and pos­i­tion, the avail­able con­ceal­ment, the observer's atten­tion, and the char­ac­ter's oppor­tun­ity shape the dif­fi­culty. manip­u­lat­ing an unat­ten­ded object beneath a crowded table is easier than remov­ing some­thing worn by an alert person in plain view.stealthusual attribute: dexterity untrained: yesstealth governs ordin­ary attempts to avoid notice through quiet move­ment, careful pos­i­tion­ing, con­trolled noise, and the use of con­ceal­ment. a char­ac­ter may choose a route that stays behind cover, wait for a guard's atten­tion to turn, cross a noisy surface care­fully, keep equip­ment from strik­ing together, or coordin­ate a group's move­ment through dark­ness or dis­trac­tion.a stealth attempt begins from cir­cum­stances that provide a plaus­ible route or place to remain unnoticed, such as cover, dark­ness, dis­trac­tion, or broken lines of sight. changes in those cir­cum­stances may create a new oppor­tun­ity, expose the char­ac­ter, or alter what con­tin­ued con­ceal­ment requires.the observer's atten­tion and the char­ac­ter's method determ­ine whether the check is unop­posed or opposed under the ordin­ary check rules. moving across noisy ground, passing close to an alert guard, or con­ceal­ing more than one person may change the dif­fi­culty.related talents: hide and sneak. both build on stealth for excep­tional con­ceal­ment and quiet move­ment.survivalusual attribute: wisdom untrained: yessur­vival covers living and trav­el­ling safely beyond settled places. it may be used to find food and water, make a defens­ible or weather­proof camp, protect sup­plies from the ele­ments, judge approach­ing weather, identify natural hazards, and choose a prac­tical line of travel through dif­fi­cult country.sur­vival also sup­ports delib­er­ate exam­in­a­tion of phys­ical tracks when usable signs remain. foot­prints, dis­turbed soil, broken veget­a­tion, dung, ashes, and dis­carded mater­ial may reveal a dir­ec­tion of travel and other con­clu­sions jus­ti­fied by the sur­viv­ing evid­ence. poor ground, weather, age, con­ceal­ment, and inter­rup­ted signs can make the task more dif­fi­cult or limit what can reas­on­ably be learned.nav­ig­a­tion determ­ines pos­i­tion and course. sur­vival keeps people sup­plied and safe while cross­ing the terrain.related talent: track­ing. track­ing builds on sur­vival for rapid recog­ni­tion and pursuit of usable signs.skill mastery: survivalsur­vival skill mastery unlocks trail recon­struc­tion. a char­ac­ter with this mastery can recon­struct the likely route between sep­ar­ated sur­viv­ing signs and reac­quire a trail after its con­tinu­ous trace has been lost, con­cealed, or delib­er­ately broken, provided enough phys­ical evid­ence remains.trail recon­struc­tion takes the time appro­pri­ate to careful exam­in­a­tion. it can bridge gaps jus­ti­fied by sur­viv­ing signs, but it cannot create evid­ence where no usable signs remain.track­ing retains its extraordin­ary speed of recog­ni­tion and pursuit. trail­craft remains a sep­ar­ate scout feature. it grants its listed +4 to par­tic­u­lar sur­vival checks for food, water, shelter, weather, and natural travel hazards; the bonus does not extend to trail recon­struc­tion, fol­low­ing tracks, nav­ig­a­tion, or avoid­ing becom­ing lost.additional skills and fieldsthe cata­logue presents common recur­ring skills rather than every field that can exist. when a new dis­cip­line becomes import­ant during play, the dm may intro­duce an appro­pri­ate skill or know­ledge field; a char­ac­ter is not pen­al­ized for lacking a skill that had not pre­vi­ously existed as an avail­able choice.90skills · sense motive – additional skills and fields
